How to use the simulator

1 Quick start · 2 Top bar · 3 Tabs · 4 DCS console · 5 Faceplates · 6 Trends and alarms · 7 SIS · 8 Field · 9 Exercises · 10 Tuning lab · 11 Debrief and data export · 12 Symbols and colours

1 · Quick start

  1. Click anywhere once so the browser allows alarm sound. Check the top bar shows 🔔 Sound on.
  2. The session opens at design: 16 m³/h of cold butane/hexane feed (35 wt% butane) is heated to 74 °C in E-400 with hot oil, let down through FCV-400 and flashed in D-400 at 102.7 kPa g. About 17 % of it leaves the top as butane-rich vapour; the rest leaves the bottom as hexane-rich liquid. Open P&ID to see the plant, then DCS console to operate it.
  3. Go to Exercises, pick a list (Training, Think EQUIPPED, Procedures or Tuning) and click Load. A blue banner gives the situation; click Acknowledge on the banner to hide it.
  4. Operate from the DCS console: click an instrument bubble, a valve or the drum to open its faceplate on the right. Hand valves are also on the Field tab, with the gauge glass, local gauges, laboratory and telephone.
  5. Use Speed to run faster (2×–50×) and Freeze to pause while you think. Flows respond in seconds, the hot-feed temperature in about a minute, the drum pressure and level in several minutes.
  6. Use the Tuning lab for bump tests, tuning rules and graded loop tests. When finished, open Debrief and grading, then Data export for CSV files for your report.

4 · DCS console

  • Overview: every loop, and a three-column summary under the drawing (feed and heating, drum and products, SIS, PSV, money).
  • Component flows: butane and hexane in the feed, the vapour and the liquid (kg/s), wt% and the component balances — the classic display of the legacy module.
  • Phase behaviour: the T–x–y diagram of butane/hexane at the present drum pressure with the operating point, the tie line (liquid AI-410, vapour AI-420) and the hot feed.
  • Control loops: mode, PV, SP, OUT, valve position and tuning of all six controllers, Rev A or Rev B.
  • Profitability: dollars per hour and totals for feed, products (on or off spec), heat, flare and N2.

Instrument bubbles follow ISA style: letters on top, loop number below, live value next to it, controller mode (MAN, AUTO, CAS, IMAN) at upper right. A red value is in alarm; a flashing value is not yet acknowledged. A square around a bubble marks an SIS switch with its own sensor (LSHH-416, LSLL-417, PSHH-426). FT-405 and FT-410 become FIC-405 and FIC-410 in Rev B.

9 · Exercises

  • Load an exercise: the plant is reset to its starting state; faults appear on their own schedule.
  • Procedure tracker: steps tick with their time when the simulator sees them done (! = done out of order). Tick Communicated and press Finish and grade (it also grades itself at the time limit).
  • Tuning exercises open the Tuning lab with the loop, the task and the graded parts; press Submit exercise for grading when done.
  • What-if, Trend matching, Scrambles, DCS reading sheet: as labelled; each result goes to the Debrief tab.

10 · Tuning lab

  1. Choose the loop and the configuration (Rev A single loops, Rev B cascades). The live trend shows PV, SP and OUT for the last 10 minutes.
  2. Bump test: the lab puts the loop in MAN, records 20 s of baseline, steps OUT by your step size and records until the duration ends (or you stop it). Hover over the plot to read time after the step, PV (engineering units and % of span) and OUT. Read K (Δ%PV/Δ%OUT), τ and θ — for the level loop the slope K* (%/s per % OUT) and θ — and press Check my model. The lab fits its own model by least squares and draws it dashed.
  3. Tuning rule: pick a rule (Ziegler–Nichols, Cohen–Coon, IMC/lambda, lambda for integrating processes, closed-loop ZN and Tyreus–Luyben from Ku and Pu). Calculate Kc, Ti, Td by hand from your model, type them and press Check my calculation, then Apply to controller.
  4. Closed-loop test: a set-point step, a +10 % feed load step, or a regulation period with a disturbance. The lab reports overshoot, rise and settling time, decay ratio, IAE, maximum deviation, recovery, valve travel and, for the level, the fastest change of the bottoms flow. The last four tests are overlaid so you can compare tunings.

11 · Debrief and data export

  • Debrief: score with each deduction, performance, exercise grades (procedures, tuning, what-if…), fault recovery times and the event log (filter and copy).
  • Data export: tick the data sets, choose range and interval, then download. The unit snapshot lists every key point against design. Files are UTF-8 CSV with # header lines. Nothing is kept after you close the page.

1 · The process at a glance

D-400 splits a liquid mixture of n-butane (C4, boils at −0.5 °C) and n-hexane (C6, boils at 69 °C) into two products in one step. The cold feed is heated under pressure in E-400, then let down through FCV-400 into the drum. At the lower pressure part of the hot liquid boils off. The vapour is rich in butane and goes to the fuel-gas header. The liquid is rich in hexane and goes to the downstream unit.

Stream numbers ◇1–◇7 match the stream table in section 5. Blue: process liquid; blue-green dashes: two-phase mixture; green: vapour; red: hot oil.

FeedHeatSeparationProducts
16 m³/h, 35 wt% butane, 10 °C, from tankage under pump pressureE-400: hot oil 180 °C heats the feed to 74 °C (about 420 kW)FCV-400 drops the pressure to 102.7 kPa g; D-400 separates vapour and liquid at 49 °CVapour ≈ 17 wt% of the feed, ≥ 75 wt% butane · Liquid ≈ 83 wt%, ≤ 28 wt% butane

2 · Working principle

2.1 One equilibrium stage

A flash drum is the simplest separation in the plant: one equilibrium stage. The feed is brought to a temperature and pressure where it is part liquid and part vapour. Given time and interface area, the two phases reach equilibrium, and the drum then only has to keep them apart. The more volatile component (butane) goes preferentially into the vapour and the less volatile (hexane) stays in the liquid.

How well it separates is set by the relative volatility, α = KC4/KC6 = PsatC4/PsatC6. At 49 °C, α ≈ 9.2: butane is nine times more willing to be in the vapour. One stage cannot give pure products, however large α is. The vapour still holds about 23 wt% hexane and the liquid about 27 wt% butane. For sharper products a column (many stages) is needed.

2.2 Phase equilibrium (Raoult's law)

Pisat(T): ln Psat [kPa] = A − B / (T [°C] + C) Ki = yi / xi = Pisat(T) / P Bubble point: xC4·PsatC4 + xC6·PsatC6 = P Dew point: yC4/PsatC4 + yC6/PsatC6 = 1/P

Butane and hexane are both straight-chain alkanes, so the ideal-solution (Raoult) model is a good approximation. For the feed (44.4 mol% butane) at the drum pressure of 204 kPa abs, the bubble point is about 43 °C and the dew point about 76 °C. A feed between these two temperatures at that pressure is two-phase. The hot feed at 74 °C is near the dew point, so a large part of the moles can vaporise. The flash then cools it, as described in 2.4.

2.3 Material balance and the lever rule

Total: F = V + L Butane: F·z = V·y + L·x Lever rule: V/F = (z − x) / (y − x) Rachford–Rice: Σ zi(Ki − 1) / (1 + (V/F)(Ki − 1)) = 0

On the T–x–y diagram the flash point sits on a horizontal tie line between the liquid composition x (bubble curve) and the vapour composition y (dew curve). The feed composition z divides the tie line: the vapour fraction is the length from z to x over the whole length. At design: z = 0.444, x = 0.349, y = 0.831 (mole fractions), so V/F = (0.444 − 0.349)/(0.831 − 0.349) ≈ 0.20 mol/mol, or 16.8 % by mass.

2.4 Energy balance: an adiabatic flash

Across FCV-400 and D-400 (no heat added): F·hF(Thot feed) = V·HV(Tflash) + L·hL(Tflash) Heat to boil the vapour comes from the feed's own sensible heat, so the flash cools: Tflash < Thot feed

No heat is added in the drum. All the heat that boils the vapour was put into the liquid in E-400 as sensible heat. When the pressure falls across FCV-400, the liquid is superheated relative to its new boiling point. Part of it boils off, taking latent heat (≈ 19 kJ/mol for butane, 30 kJ/mol for hexane) out of the remaining liquid, until everything is back on the saturation curve. The mixture cools from 74 °C to about 49 °C. E-400 is therefore the energy input to the separation. More duty gives more vapour.

2.5 Why the pressure is let down after heating

E-400 is kept full of liquid. Upstream of FCV-400 the pressure is about 550 kPa g, well above the bubble pressure of the hot feed at 74 °C (about 360 kPa g). No vapour forms in the exchanger tubes, so there is no vapour blanketing and no slug flow. Flashing happens in and after the let-down valve, where the drum gives the vapour room to disengage.

2.6 The two handles: temperature and pressure

For a fixed feed, the split and both compositions depend on two variables. The operator sets the hot-feed temperature with TIC-401 and the drum pressure with PIC-420:

  • Hotter feed: more vapour, and the extra vapour carries more hexane (AI-420 falls). The liquid loses butane (AI-410 falls). The flash temperature rises.
  • Higher drum pressure: less vapour; a purer vapour (AI-420 rises) but a liquid richer in butane (AI-410 rises). The flash temperature rises.
  • The two product specifications pull in opposite directions (vapour ≥ 75 wt% butane, liquid ≤ 28 wt% butane). The operating window is the band of temperature and pressure where both are met. Use the calculator below to find its edges.

The drum level (LIC-400) and the feed flow (FIC-400) do not change the equilibrium. The level is a buffer that absorbs flow changes and protects the vapour line and the downstream unit.

3 · Flash calculator (steady state)

An adiabatic flash with the simulator's own thermodynamics. Move the sliders to see the split, both product compositions and the T–x–y diagram at the chosen drum pressure. It is off-line: it does not change the running plant. It assumes full equilibrium; the live drum reaches slightly less vapour (about 611 instead of 619 Nm³/h) because it approaches equilibrium at a finite evaporation rate.

6 · Process description

6.1 Feed system

Butane/hexane feed (stream 1, 35 wt% butane, 10 °C) comes from tankage at about 650 kPa g. It passes the SIS shut-off valve XV-408 (fails closed) and the orifice flow element FT-400, which measures the cold liquid for FIC-400. FIC-400 holds the feed at 16 m³/h by moving FCV-400. FCV-400 sits downstream of E-400, so one valve sets the feed rate and also takes the pressure let-down. TI-400 reads the cold-feed temperature.

6.2 Feed preheater E-400

The feed flows through the tubes of the shell-and-tube exchanger E-400. Hot oil at 180 °C from the utility header flows through the shell, counter-current. The 3-way valve TCV-401 splits the hot oil between E-400 and a bypass. At design, 30.5 % of the header flow (FI-405 ≈ 11 t/h) goes through the shell and returns at about 120 °C (TI-403), giving about 420 kW. TIC-401 measures the hot feed at the exchanger outlet (TT-401) and moves TCV-401 (reverse acting: too hot → less oil through E-400). On air failure TCV-401 sends all the oil to bypass (fail-safe: no heat). TI-402 and PDI-406 show the hot-oil header temperature and pressure difference. They explain most upsets that start on the utility side. The hot feed (stream 2, 74 °C) stays liquid because its pressure is well above its bubble pressure.

6.3 Let-down and flash

Across FCV-400 (fails closed) the pressure falls from about 550 to 102.7 kPa g. The liquid partly vaporises and cools to about 49 °C (stream 3, two-phase). Block valve HV-401 and its bypass HV-402 isolate the line. The globe valve HV-403 lets the operator throttle the feed by hand when FCV-400 is out of service.

6.4 Flash drum D-400

The two-phase feed enters the vertical drum D-400 (1.6 m ID × 4.8 m tangent to tangent, about 10.7 m³). The inlet momentum is broken and the phases separate by gravity. Liquid collects in the lower part, where about 18 minutes of hold-up at 50 % level lets gas bubbles escape. Vapour rises through the mesh pad, which catches entrained droplets. The upward vapour velocity is only a few centimetres per second, far below the flooding limit, so carry-over appears only with foaming or an overfilled drum. TI-410 reads the flash temperature. LT-400 (for LIC-400) and the gauge glass LG-400 show the level. The SIS switches LSHH-416 and LSLL-417 and the pressure switch PSHH-426 have their own sensors.

6.5 Vapour product

Vapour (stream 4) leaves the top through FI-420 and analyser AI-420. It goes through the pressure-control valve PCV-420 (fails open) and block valve HV-421 to the fuel-gas header at about 30 kPa g. PIC-420 is direct acting: higher pressure → PCV-420 opens. PSV-400, set at 450 kPa g, relieves to flare if the vapour outlet is blocked and the SIS fails. HV-422 bypasses HV-421 and HV-423 bypasses PCV-420.

6.6 Liquid product

Liquid (stream 5) leaves the bottom through the SIS valve XV-418, flow element FT-410 and analyser AI-410. It then passes the level-control valve LCV-400 (fails closed) and block valve HV-411 to the downstream unit at about 40 kPa g. LIC-400 is direct acting (level up → LCV-400 opens) and tuned for averaging: the level may drift within its band so the flow to the downstream unit changes slowly. HV-412 bypasses HV-411, HV-413 throttles around LCV-400, and HV-415 drains the drum to the closed drain.

6.7 Nitrogen blanket

When there is no vapour production (start-up, shutdown, hot-oil failure), the regulator PCV-430 admits N2 (through HV-430) to hold the drum at about 30 kPa g. This keeps air out and keeps a positive pressure on the drum. In normal operation the drum pressure is far above 30 kPa g, so PCV-430 stays shut and AI-400 reads no N2. Nitrogen in the vapour means the regulator is passing or the drum was not swept after a start-up.

6.8 Control configurations

Rev A (the original design) has four single loops: FIC-400, TIC-401 → TCV-401, LIC-400 → LCV-400 and PIC-420 → PCV-420. Rev B adds two cascades. TIC-401 sets the hot-oil flow set point of FIC-405, which then moves TCV-401 and rejects hot-oil header swings before they reach the feed temperature. LIC-400 sets the bottoms-flow set point of FIC-410, which rejects downstream pressure swings. Switch between them on the Tuning lab or Instructor station.

6.9 Safety instrumented system

I-1 (LSHH-416 at 90 % or PSHH-426 at 250 kPa g, or the ESD pushbutton) closes XV-408 (feed) and XV-409 (hot oil). This stops the feed and the heat together. I-2 (LSLL-417 at 5 %) closes XV-418 so gas cannot blow through to the downstream unit. Both latch and must be reset by the operator after the cause is removed. PSV-400 is the last layer.

6.10 Start-up and shutdown in one paragraph

Start-up: line up the block valves; reset the SIS and open XV-408 and XV-409; put PIC-420 in AUTO at about 70 % of design pressure. Start the feed at about half rate and warm it by hand before putting TIC-401 in AUTO at 74 °C. Sweep the N2 out with the first vapour. Once the level is above 15 % reset I-2 and open XV-418, then put LIC-400 in AUTO. Raise the pressure set point to 102.7 kPa g and the feed in steps to 16 m³/h. Shutdown is the reverse order: feed, heat, pressure, level, drain, isolate. Full graded procedures are on the Exercises tab.

Trainee workbook · Flash Drum Ver 1

Work through Parts A to H in order. Record your answers and evidence (screenshots, CSV files) as you go; your report is built from them.

1 Purpose · 2 The unit · 3 Control scheme · 4 Safety systems · 5 Operating rules · 6 Activities A–H · 7 Grading · 8 Report checklist

1 · Purpose

A flash drum is the simplest separation in the plant: one equilibrium stage. By the end you should be able to:

  1. Operate the flash drum as an outside operator and as a console operator: read the P&ID and the DCS and state the normal value and alarm limits of every key tag.
  2. Explain with the T–x–y diagram and the lever rule how feed temperature and drum pressure set the vapour fraction and both product compositions.
  3. Close the material balance, total and by component, from the DCS indications.
  4. Start up through the SIS and shut down safely and in order.
  5. Identify a loop from a bump test (K, τ, θ; or an integrating slope), tune it with a named rule, and prove the tuning with a closed-loop test; choose between tight and averaging level control; use a cascade to reject a supply disturbance.
  6. Recognise an abnormal situation from alarms, trends and field checks, keep the unit safe, and find the root cause with a systematic six-stage method.

2 · The unit

Cold feed (butane/hexane, 10 °C) from tankage passes the SIS valve XV-408 and flow meter FT-400 into the tubes of E-400, where hot oil on the shell heats it to 74 °C (TIC-401). The 3-way valve TCV-401 sends part of the hot oil through E-400 and the rest around it. The hot liquid is still under pressure; it is let down through FCV-400 (FIC-400) and block valve HV-401 into the vertical drum D-400, where part of it flashes. The flash cools the stream to about 49 °C. Vapour rises through the mesh pad and leaves on pressure control (PIC-420 → PCV-420, block valve HV-421) to the fuel-gas header; liquid leaves on level control (LIC-400 → LCV-400, SIS valve XV-418, block valve HV-411) to the downstream unit. A nitrogen regulator PCV-430 keeps the drum above 30 kPa g when there is no vapour.

Values are the model's design point with noise off. Feed flow, feed temperature, hot-feed temperature, drum pressure, level and controller outputs are those of the original training booklet; the product flows, compositions and flash temperature are calculated from them (ideal-solution vapour–liquid equilibrium, adiabatic flash) and agree with the booklet within a few percent. The hot-oil conditions, drum size, supply and header pressures, SIS, PSV, N2 blanket, globe bypasses and the Rev B cascades are engineering assumptions and teaching additions.

3 · Control scheme

ConfigurationTemperatureLevelWhy
Rev A (legacy)TIC-401 → TCV-401LIC-400 → LCV-400Simple; any change in hot-oil header pressure or downstream pressure upsets the loop before the controller can see it.
Rev B (cascade)TIC-401 → FIC-405 SP → TCV-401LIC-400 → FIC-410 SP → LCV-400The fast inner flow loop corrects supply and back-pressure swings in seconds; the outer loop only trims. Tune the slave first, then the master with the slave in CAS.

Fail positions: FCV-400 and LCV-400 fail closed, TCV-401 fails to full bypass (no heat), PCV-420 fails open (drum relieves to the header), XVs fail closed.

4 · Safety systems

SIS I-1 closes the feed XV-408 and the hot oil XV-409 on high-high level (LSHH-416), high-high pressure (PSHH-426) or ESD. SIS I-2 closes the bottoms XV-418 on low-low level (LSLL-417) so gas cannot blow through into the downstream unit. The switches have their own sensors: a frozen LT-400 or a biased PT-420 does not defeat them. PSV-400 relieves to flare at 450 kPa g.

Alarm limits

5 · Operating rules

  1. Never block in the overhead with feed and heat on: the pressure climbs about 10 kPa per minute to the PSHH trip.
  2. Level between 30 and 70 %. High level wets the mesh pad and carries liquid into the fuel gas; low level lets gas blow through to the downstream unit.
  3. Pressure and temperature set the split. Hotter feed or lower pressure → more vapour, and both products get heavier. Keep AI-410 ≤ 28 and AI-420 ≥ 75 wt% butane.
  4. Hot oil on only with feed flowing: never heat a blocked-in exchanger.
  5. Trust two independent readings over one transmitter: gauge glass vs LT-400, PG-420 vs PT-420, TI-410 vs TIC-401, lab vs analyzer.
  6. Tune one loop at a time, with the plant steady, and write down the old settings first. In Rev B tune the slave before the master.
  7. Butane is extremely flammable and heavier than air: report any leak, never vent to atmosphere.

6 · Activities

Part A · Identification (about 1 h)

  1. Open the P&ID sheets. Trace feed, hot oil, vapour, liquid, N2, flare and drain lines and list every instrument and valve on each. Explain every fail position.
  2. Visit the five DCS displays and the Field tab. For every valve write its normal state.
  3. Complete the DCS reading sheet (Exercises tab). Graded out of 15.
  4. Take lab samples and download a unit snapshot CSV. Close the component balances.

Part B · Normal operations: what-if (about 30 min per event)

For each event predict ↑ / ↓ / = for all eight variables 30 minutes after the event before pressing Check my predictions. Explain every wrong prediction with the T–x–y diagram, the lever rule, a heat balance or the level loop.

Part C · Cold startup (graded, limit 2 h simulated)

Load Cold startup from Procedures. The tracker ticks steps as you complete them. Filling the drum at half rate takes most of the time (a careful startup takes about 80–90 simulated minutes), so run at 5–10× while you wait for the level:

    Part D · Training exercises (troubleshooting A: cause and effect)

    Before each exercise write what you expect to change (process, alarms, controllers, indicators, equipment state), the safety concerns and whom to contact. Then run it and record: first alarm and time, the first variable you noticed, what you did, and the recovery time in Debrief.

    Part E · Think EQUIPPED troubleshooting

    Each case gives only a situation. Work through the six stages and write your evidence for each (EQUIPPED = Equipment, Utilities, Instrumentation, Process, People, Environment, Downstream/upstream):

    StageWhat you must produce
    1 EngageIs it dangerous or time-critical (overpressure, overfill, gas blow-by, off-spec product)? Decide: keep running, cut feed, or shut down, and state what would change your mind.
    2 DefineProblem statement (what, where, when, how much, what did not change), IS / IS NOT table, the time line, and a measurable target.
    3 ExploreFundamentals: the flash (T–x–y, lever rule), the component balance, the heat balance on E-400, the pressure–flow of each valve. Compare instruments, list recent changes, list EQUIPPED causes.
    4 PlanAt least three working hypotheses written so they can fail, each with a test (tag, field check, lab sample, phone call, what result kills it), ordered by safety, time and cost.
    5 Do itRun the tests, record results, name the root cause, apply the fix; predict the response before each move.
    6 Look backCompare prediction with result, and propose a change that stops it happening again.

    Part F · Trend matching, scrambles, troubleshooting B and C, emergencies

    Match four unlabelled trend sets to their events and justify each from the six pens. Put the startup, shutdown and LT-400 scrambles in order, then run the graded Troubleshooting B (LT-400 failure), Troubleshooting C (more vapour with an unknown upset) and the two emergencies from Procedures.

    Part G · Loop tuning (Tuning lab)

    Complete the tuning exercises. For each loop record: the bump test (step size, K, τ, θ with your graphical construction), the rule and the numbers you calculated, the closed-loop test results before and after, and what you would recommend to the plant.

    Part H · Optimisation, data and report

    Run the 40-minute optimisation. For your startup, one tuning exercise and one troubleshooting case download the run data (all data sets, 5 s), the unit snapshot and the event log. Plot FIC-400, TIC-401, PIC-420, LIC-400, FI-410 and FI-420 against time, and the component balance before and after.

        Control loops and tuning · the basics

        The ideas behind the six controllers of D-400 and behind every exercise in the Tuning lab. Read sections 1–3 before the first bump test and 4–6 before choosing a tuning rule.

        1 The feedback loop · 2 The loops of D-400 · 3 The PID controller · 4 Process dynamics · 5 Tuning rules · 6 Judging a tuning · 7 Loop simulator · 8 Worked example: TIC-401 · 9 Level, cascade, valves

        1 · The feedback loop

        TermMeaningExample: TIC-401
        PV (process variable)The measured value the loop controlsHot-feed temperature from TT-401, °C
        SP (set point)Where the operator (or a master controller) wants the PV74 °C
        Error eSP − PV (reverse acting) or PV − SP (direct acting)74 − 73.2 = +0.8 °C
        OUT (MV, controller output)The signal to the final element, 0–100 %TCV-401 signal, 30.5 % at design
        Final elementWhat physically changes the process3-way valve splitting hot oil between E-400 and bypass
        Disturbance (load)Anything else that moves the PVFeed rate, hot-oil temperature or header pressure, fouling
        • Feedback acts only after the PV has moved. It cannot beat the process dead time, but it corrects every disturbance, including ones nobody measured.
        • Action. A reverse-acting controller lowers OUT when the PV rises. Use it when opening the valve raises the PV (TIC-401: more oil → hotter; FIC-400: open → more flow). A direct-acting controller raises OUT when the PV rises. Use it when opening the valve lowers the PV (LIC-400: open LCV → level falls; PIC-420: open PCV → pressure falls). The wrong action makes positive feedback: the valve runs to its limit.
        • Fail-safe position is chosen for the process, not for the controller. FCV-400, LCV-400 and the XVs fail closed; PCV-420 fails open so the drum cannot be blocked in; TCV-401 fails to full bypass so no heat goes in.
        • Modes. MAN: the operator sets OUT. AUTO: the controller sets OUT to hold the SP. CAS: the SP comes from another controller. Changing mode is bumpless: the controller starts from the current OUT, so the valve does not jump.

        2 · The loops of D-400 and their character

        The identified models come from bump tests on this simulator at design (K in % of PV span per % OUT). They change with the operating point: at half the feed rate TIC-401 has a larger gain and a longer dead time. With the design tuning it cycles below about 6 m³/h, which is why the start-up procedure feeds at 7–9 m³/h.

        3 · The PID controller

        All controllers here use the ISA standard (ideal) form, positional, in % of span:

        OUT(t) = Kc · [ e(t) + (1/Ti)·∫e dt − Td · dPV/dt ] + bias e, PV, OUT in % of span; Kc in %/%; Ti, Td in seconds Ti = 0 means no integral action. Derivative acts on the PV (not on the error), so a set-point step gives no derivative kick.
        ModeWhat it doesToo littleToo much
        P (gain Kc)OUT moves in proportion to the error, at onceSluggish, large deviation after a disturbanceOscillation; on noisy loops the valve chatters
        I (reset time Ti)Keeps moving OUT while any error remains, which removes offset. A shorter Ti means stronger integral action.Long Ti: the PV creeps back to SP slowlyShort Ti: overshoot and slow oscillation; worst on processes with dead time
        D (rate time Td)Acts on the rate of change of the PV and anticipates—Amplifies noise; useless on flow and level loops
        • Offset with P only. A proportional controller needs an error to hold a new OUT. With Ti = 0 the PV settles away from SP, and the offset shrinks as Kc grows. The integral term removes it.
        • Reset windup. If the valve is at 0 or 100 % while an error persists, the integral keeps growing. When the error reverses, the valve stays saturated until that integral unwinds. These controllers clamp the integral (anti-windup) when OUT hits a limit.
        • Gain in % of span. Kc = 1 means that a 1 % of span error moves OUT by 1 %. Change a transmitter range and the effective loop gain changes too.

        4 · Process dynamics: what a bump test tells you

        Self-regulating (FOPDT). After a step in OUT the PV settles at a new value. Flow, temperature and pressure behave like this. Three numbers describe it:

        • K, process gain = ΔPV% / ΔOUT% (after it settles)
        • θ, dead time: from the step until the PV starts to move
        • τ, time constant: speed of the response after the dead time (63 % of the change is reached at θ + τ)
        G(s) = K·e−θs / (τs + 1) Two-point method: t28 and t63 = times after the step to 28.3 % and 63.2 % of ΔPV τ = 1.5 (t63 − t28) θ = t63 − τ

        Integrating. With the outlet valve fixed, a level keeps rising (or falling) as long as inflow and outflow differ. There is no new steady state, only a slope: K* = (dPV%/dt) / ΔOUT% in %/s per %.

        G(s) = K*·e−θs / s
        • Controllability ratio θ/τ. Below 0.2 the loop is easy (tight tuning possible). Around 0.3 (TIC-401) it is moderate. Above 1 dead time dominates and feedback must be slow.
        • Good bump-test practice: start at steady state in MAN. Step OUT by 3–10 % (enough to see through the noise, small enough to stay in the alarm band). Wait until the PV has settled (4–5 τ + θ). If possible, repeat in the other direction to see non-linearity.

        5 · Tuning rules

        RuleNeedsPI settingsCharacter
        Ziegler–Nichols, reaction curveK, τ, θKc = 0.9τ/(Kθ) · Ti = 3.33θAggressive, aims at quarter-amplitude decay; often ringing
        Cohen–CoonK, τ, θKc = (1/K)(τ/θ)(0.9 + θ/12τ) · Ti = θ(30 + 3θ/τ)/(9 + 20θ/τ)Aggressive; better for larger θ/τ; good load rejection
        IMC / lambdaK, τ, θ, chosen λKc = τ/(K(λ + θ)) · Ti = τYou choose the closed-loop time constant λ. λ = τ is a robust start; λ ≥ θ always.
        Lambda, integrating (level)K*, θ, arrest time λKc = (2λ + θ)/(K*(λ + θ)²) · Ti = 2λ + θλ is how long the level takes to stop a disturbance. Long λ = averaging.
        Ziegler–Nichols, closed loopKu, PuKc = 0.45Ku · Ti = Pu/1.2No model needed, but the loop must be driven to the edge of stability
        Tyreus–LuybenKu, PuKc = Ku/3.2 · Ti = 2.2PuConservative version of ZN closed loop; little overshoot

        Ultimate gain test. With P-only control (Ti = 0, Td = 0), raise Kc in steps, bumping the SP each time. At Ku the PV oscillates with constant amplitude; Pu is the period of that oscillation. Do this only where a sustained oscillation is acceptable.

        PID versions (the Tuning lab also offers ZN-PID, Cohen–Coon PID, IMC-PID and ZN closed-loop PID) add derivative for loops with a large lag and little noise. None of the D-400 loops really needs it.

        6 · Judging a tuning

        MeasureDefinition
        OvershootPeak beyond the new SP, as % of the SP step
        Rise time10 % to 90 % of the SP step
        Settling timeUntil the PV stays within ±5 % of the step
        Decay ratioSecond peak / first peak (ZN aims at 0.25)
        IAE∫|SP − PV| dt: total error, in %·s
        Max deviation, recoveryFor a load step: largest error, and time to return within a band
        Valve travelTotal OUT movement: wear and upset of other loops

        Set-point tracking and load rejection are different jobs. Operators rarely move set points but disturbances arrive all the time, so judge a loop mainly on load steps. A slow integral (long Ti) tracks set points without overshoot but leaves load errors lasting a long time (TU-10).

        Is it the tuning, the valve or a disturbance? Put the loop in MAN for a few minutes:

        • Cycling stops → the controller causes it (too aggressive, or a sticking valve inside the loop).
        • Cycling continues → a disturbance from outside (hot-oil header swings, downstream pressure swings).
        • In AUTO the OUT is a saw-tooth and the PV a square wave → valve stiction. Retuning will not cure it; a longer Ti only slows the cycle.

        7 · Loop simulator (off-line)

        A first-order-plus-dead-time or integrating process under PI(D) control, independent of the plant. Shortly after the start the set point steps +5 %. Halfway through the run a load disturbance equal to −5 % of OUT enters at the process input. Try the rules on a model, then prove them on the real loop in the Tuning lab.

        Apply a rule:

        8 · Worked example: tuning TIC-401 from a bump test

        1. Test. TIC-401 to MAN at OUT 30.5 %. Step OUT to 35.5 % (+5 %). The hot-feed temperature starts to rise after about 14 s and settles about 4.1 °C higher.
        2. Gain in % of span. The range is 0–150 °C, so ΔPV = 4.1/150 × 100 = 2.75 %. K = 2.75/5 ≈ 0.55 %/%.
        3. Time constant and dead time. t28 ≈ 29 s and t63 ≈ 59 s after the step, so τ = 1.5 × (59 − 29) = 45 s and θ = 59 − 45 = 14 s. θ/τ ≈ 0.3.
        4. Rules:

        Test each with a +5 °C set-point step and a +10 % feed step. ZN and Cohen–Coon settle fast but overshoot and ring. IMC with λ = τ is almost free of overshoot and robust to the gain rising at low feed rates. The installed tuning (Kc 1.4, Ti 55 s) is close to IMC. For better load rejection IMC with λ ≈ 0.5τ is a good compromise (exercise TU-10).

        9 · Level control, cascades and valves

        9.1 Tight or averaging level control

        A level loop has two possible jobs. Tight control holds the level close to its set point, so every inflow change passes straight to the outflow. Averaging control uses the drum volume as a surge tank: the level may move within its band (35–65 %) so the flow to the downstream unit changes slowly. D-400 feeds another unit, so LIC-400 is tuned for averaging, with an arrest time of about 10 minutes (Kc ≈ 1.5, Ti ≈ 1200 s). Very low gain combined with a short Ti makes a slow oscillation. For an integrating process keep Kc·Ti large (for the lambda rule Kc·Ti·K* ≈ 4 or more).

        9.2 Cascade control (Rev B)

        • The master (TIC-401, LIC-400) sets the SP of the slave (FIC-405, FIC-410). The slave moves the valve.
        • The slave corrects disturbances in its own loop (hot-oil header pressure, downstream pressure) before they reach the master's PV.
        • The slave must be at least 3–5 times faster than the master. Tune the slave first, in AUTO. Then put it in CAS and tune the master, using the slave's closed loop as part of the process.
        • When the slave is not in CAS the master goes to IMAN and tracks, so switching back is bumpless.

        9.3 The valve is part of the loop

        • Equal-percentage valves (all control valves here) have a small gain when nearly closed and a large gain near fully open. A loop tuned at 30 % opening responds differently at 80 %.
        • Stiction (sticky packing) causes a dead band. The controller winds up until the valve jumps, which gives a limit cycle whatever the tuning (TU-7, TE-9).
        • Saturation: a valve at 0 or 100 % means the loop has lost control. No tuning can help; find out why the valve ran out of range.

        Loop

        Live trend, last 10 min: PV blue (left axis), SP grey dashed, OUT orange (right axis 0–100 %).

        1Bump test (open loop) and model

        The loop goes to MAN; 20 s baseline, then the step.

        Move the mouse over the plot to read time, PV and OUT.

        Two-point method: t28 and t63 are the times after the step at which the PV has made 28.3 % and 63.2 % of its total change; τ = 1.5 (t63 − t28), θ = t63 − τ. K uses % of span: ΔPV% = ΔPV / span × 100.

        3Closed-loop test

        2Tuning rule

        Ultimate gain (closed-loop Ziegler–Nichols)

        P-only (Ti = 0): raise Kc in steps, bump the SP each time, until the oscillation neither grows nor decays. Ku = that gain; Pu = period of the oscillation (s).

        Good practice

        • Steady plant first; note the old tuning; one loop at a time.
        • Bump big enough to see through the noise (3–10 %), small enough to stay inside the alarms.
        • Flow loops: fast and noisy — small Kc, short Ti. Temperature: dead time matters — keep Kc·K·θ/τ modest.
        • Level: decide first — tight (protect the drum) or averaging (protect the downstream unit).
        • Pressure over a boiling liquid: two time scales — tune on the slow one, check the fast one does not ring.
        • A cycling loop is not always tuning: MAN test — if the cycle stops and OUT is a saw-tooth, suspect the valve.

        How a flash drum like D-400 is specified and roughed out before detailed design. Every number below is computed in this page from the simulator's own thermodynamics (Antoine + Raoult, adiabatic flash), its design constants and its alarm and trip table, at the design case (16 m³/h feed, 35 wt% butane, 74 °C hot feed, 102.7 kPa g). The sizing in part 5 is conceptual: rules of thumb and short-cut correlations, not a vendor or detailed mechanical design.

        1 Fundamentals · 2 Components · 3 Setting the operating conditions · 4 Conceptual design · 5 Conceptual sizing (calculator)

        1 · Fundamentals of the flash separator

        A flash drum is one equilibrium stage. The feed is brought to a temperature and pressure between its bubble and dew points, part of it boils, and the drum gives the two phases time and space to separate. Nine pieces of engineering decide how D-400 is designed and how it behaves; each is worked through below with the design numbers.

        1.1 Phase equilibrium: Antoine, Raoult, K-values

        ln Pisat [kPa] = Ai − Bi / (T [°C] + Ci)    yi P = xi Pisat(T)    Ki = yi/xi = Pisat/P    α = KC4/KC6 = PC4sat/PC6sat

        n-Butane and n-hexane are both straight-chain alkanes, so an ideal solution (Raoult's law) is a good model. At the flash temperature the vapour pressures are (butane) and (hexane). With the drum at the K-values are and : butane prefers the vapour, hexane the liquid. The relative volatility is , which is large; separation is easy in principle, but one stage still cannot make pure products.

        For a binary the two equilibrium compositions at a given T and P follow directly: xC4 = (1 − KC6)/(KC4 − KC6) = , yC4 = KC4 xC4 = (mol fractions; and by mass, which is what AI-410 and AI-420 read).

        1.2 Bubble point and dew point

        Bubble point: Σ zi Ki(T,P) = 1  ⇔  Σ zi Pisat(T) = P     Dew point: Σ zi/Ki(T,P) = 1

        The feed is butane (35 wt%). At the drum pressure its bubble point is and its dew point . A flash only happens between these two: the drum must be fed with a mixture whose enthalpy lies in that range. Seen the other way, the bubble pressure of the hot feed at 74 °C is . Upstream of FCV-400 the pressure is about , so E-400 runs full of liquid and the feed boils only after the let-down valve, in the drum (margin ).

        1.3 Material balance: lever rule and Rachford–Rice

        F = V + L    F zi = V yi + L xi    lever rule: β = V/F = (z − x)/(y − x)
        Rachford–Rice: Σ zi(Ki − 1) / (1 + β(Ki − 1)) = 0

        With z = , x = and y = the lever rule gives β = of the moles as vapour, or of the mass. The feed of therefore splits into about vapour (, FI-420) and liquid ( at drum conditions, FI-410). Rachford–Rice is the same balance written for many components; with two it has the closed-form solution above, which is how the simulator solves every time step.

        1.4 Adiabatic flash: why the stream cools from 74 to 49 °C

        hF(Thot) = β hV(T, y) + (1 − β) hL(T, x)    (no heat added in the valve or drum)
        cp,F (Thot − T) ≈ β λ     sensible heat released = latent heat taken up

        Nothing heats the drum. The only energy available to boil the vapour is the sensible heat the feed carries above the drum temperature. Solving the balance by trial temperature gives T = . Check: the feed gives up cpΔT = × = , and boiling of it at λ ≈ takes . The two are equal: that is why the flash temperature is fixed by the hot-feed temperature and the pressure, and why TI-410 is a result, not a set point. Hotter feed → more vapour, but the drum temperature rises only slowly because extra boiling absorbs most of the extra heat.

        1.5 E-400 duty, ε-NTU and the 3-way hot-oil valve

        Q = ṁF cp,F (Thot − Tin) = ṁoil cp,oil (Toil,in − Toil,out)
        ε = Q / (Cmin (Toil,in − Tin))    counter-current: ε = (1 − e−NTU(1−Cr)) / (1 − Cr e−NTU(1−Cr))    NTU = UA / Cmin

        Duty: × × (74 − 10) K = . With hot oil at 180 °C cooled by 60 K the oil flow is (FI-405), returning at about 120 °C (TI-403). The feed is the smaller heat-capacity stream (Cmin = , Cr = ), ε = , NTU = , so UA = and the mean temperature difference is . At an assumed U of 300 W/m² K that is about of surface.

        TCV-401 is a 3-way valve on the utility side: it sends part of the hot-oil flow through E-400 and the rest round the bypass, so the header sees a nearly constant flow whatever the duty. At design it sends of the full flow to E-400. With the valve fully to E-400 the existing exchanger could heat the design feed to about ; that is the heating margin, and it is also why the valve fails to full bypass (no heat) on loss of air.

        1.6 Vapour–liquid separation: Souders–Brown, with and without a mesh pad

        umax = Ks √((ρL − ρV) / ρV)    Dmin = √(4 QV / (π umax))

        A drop falls against the rising vapour when its weight beats the drag. The balance gives the largest vapour velocity that still lets drops of a given size settle. At the drum: ρL = , ρV = (ideal gas, M = ), QV = .

        CaseKs (typical)umaxDmin for vapourLoad in D-400 (u / umax)

        The vapour needs only a fraction of the D-400 cross-section (actual velocity ). The mesh pad doubles the allowable velocity and stops fine mist (drops of about 10 µm and up) that gravity alone would let through. Note that a mesh pad works by impaction and loses efficiency when the velocity is far below its design range (typically below about 30 % of umax); in D-400 gravity alone already handles the load, so the pad is a polishing step for the fuel-gas header. The diameter is set by the liquid, next.

        1.7 Liquid hold-up and surge time between alarm and trip levels

        t = Adrum Δh / QL    Δh = span × ΔL / 100    (time for the level to cross a band if the outflow stops, or the inflow stops)

        The level span of LT-400 is starting above the bottom tangent; the cross-section is , so one per cent of span holds . With the liquid product at :

        BandLevelsHeight above bottom tangentVolumeTime at design liquid flowWhat the time is for

        The surge time (normal level to the high alarm) and the hold-up time (low alarm to normal level) are what size the drum: D-400 gives about each way, and from NLL to the LSHH-416 trip if the liquid outlet is blocked. The whole liquid inventory at NLL is , a residence time of .

        1.8 Control valve sizing and the equal-percentage trim

        Q = Cv f(x) √(ΔP / ρ)    (mass form in the simulator: ṁ = C f(x) √(ρ ΔP))    equal-%: f(x) = Rx − 1, R = 30

        A valve is sized so that the design flow at the design pressure drop needs a mid-range opening (typically 50–80 % for equal-% trim), leaving room to open for higher flow or lower ΔP and to close for turndown. Equal-% trim gives the same relative change in flow for each per cent of stroke, which compensates for the ΔP that the valve gains as the flow falls (the pipe and exchanger losses shrink with the square of flow). Worked on the four valves with the installed capacities of the simulator (Cv in US units, 1 Cv ≈ 0.865 m³/h at 1 bar and SG 1):

        ValveFluid, flowΔP across the valveCv neededCv installed (100 %)Opening from f(x)Simulator OUTFails

        PCV-420 passes vapour; below critical flow (ΔP < ½ P1) the simulator uses the same square-root law with the vapour density, which is adequate for a conceptual size. TCV-401 is a 3-way valve with a linear split of a nearly constant hot-oil flow.

        1.9 Relief load basics (a teaching simplification)

        PSV-400 is set at the drum's maximum allowable working pressure, , and relieves to flare. The relief load is the largest vapour flow any credible single cause can generate at the relieving pressure (set + 10 % overpressure for process causes, + 21 % for fire). Two cases are worked here in the simplest form; a real study (API 520/521) considers every cause and uses rigorous properties.

        • Blocked vapour outlet (a valve in the vapour line closed). The drum pressure rises until the hot feed can no longer flash. At design the hot feed's bubble pressure is only , below the set pressure, so the pressure stops rising well before the valve lifts; PSHH-426 trips the feed at . The credible worst case adds a second failure, TCV-401 driven fully to E-400: the feed can then reach about , whose bubble pressure is . Flashed at the relieving pressure () it gives about of vapour.
        • External fire. Heat input to the wetted wall (up to 7.6 m above grade): Q = 43.2 F Awet0.82 kW (API 521 form with drainage and fire fighting, F = 1 for a bare vessel). With Awet ≈ at NLL, Q ≈ ; the liquid boils at at 121 % of set with λ ≈ , giving W = Q/λ ≈ .
        • The orifice area follows from the API 520 vapour equation A = W/(C Kd P1) √(T Z / M): about for the governing case (), i.e. a orifice. Fire governs because it can boil the whole liquid inventory, whatever the controls do.

        3 · Setting the operating conditions

        For a given feed the flash has only two thermodynamic handles, the hot-feed temperature and the drum pressure; everything else (flash temperature, vapour fraction, product compositions) follows. The other conditions are set for throughput, inventory, utilities and safety. Each value is chosen from a process requirement, then checked against an alarm or an equipment limit (read live from the page's alarm table and SIS constants).

        ConditionSet by (handle)Design valueWhy this valueLimit / alarmIf too highIf too low

        Order in which the conditions are set

        1. Pressure first. A defined drum pressure exists before any hydrocarbon arrives: the N2 blanket (PCV-430) keeps the drum above atmospheric and PIC-420 holds its set point. The flash is defined by pressure, so it must be there first.
        2. Flow next. Feed is established through FCV-400 at a reduced rate, cold, while the level builds; the liquid outlet is put on LIC-400 once the level is in the normal band.
        3. Heat only with flow. Hot oil goes to E-400 only when feed is flowing (a blocked-in, heated liquid expands and boils). TIC-401 is then raised towards 74 °C.
        4. Rate. The feed is raised to the design rate; TIC-401, LIC-400 and PIC-420 follow.
        5. Specifications. Temperature and pressure are trimmed on the product analysers (AI-420 ≥ spec, AI-410 ≤ spec), preferring the cheaper handle.
        6. Check the margins: TI-410 inside its band, level between alarms, TCV-401 and FCV-400 with room to move, AI-400 (N2) low.

        4 · Conceptual design

        4.1 Design basis

        ItemValueSource

        4.2 Design decisions

        DecisionOptionsChoice for D-400Reason

        4.3 Design sequence

        1. Specifications to operating point. From the two product specifications find the temperature–pressure pairs that meet both (the Operating windows tab maps them), then pick the pressure from the vapour destination (header 30 kPa g plus valve ΔP) and the hot-feed temperature inside the window with margin to both specs.
        2. Heat and material balance. Adiabatic flash at that point: β, x, y, flash temperature, product rates (calculator step 1).
        3. Preheater. Duty, hot-oil flow and return temperature, ε-NTU → UA → area; check the maximum hot-feed temperature with the valve fully open (step 2).
        4. Pressure profile. Supply pressure, E-400 and piping losses, FCV-400 ΔP, and the check that the hot feed stays below its bubble pressure upstream of the let-down valve.
        5. Drum. Souders–Brown → minimum diameter for vapour; surge and hold-up times → level span; add the vapour space (inlet device, disengagement, mesh pad); solve for D at the chosen H/D; take the larger diameter (steps 3–4).
        6. Nozzles and internals. Inlet momentum and inlet device, vapour and liquid outlets, vortex breaker, bridle (step 5).
        7. Control valves. Size each for a mid-range opening at design and check the high-rate case (step 6).
        8. Protection. Alarms and trips on the level ladder, relief cases and orifice, MAWP and wall thickness (step 7); then the data sheets, HAZOP and LOPA.

        5 · Conceptual sizing

        Change any input; results update immediately. Defaults reproduce the simulator's design case. The column "Simulator" shows the lined-out simulator values (from the design snapshot) or its installed equipment. Checks marked ✗ are outside the usual guideline or an alarm limit of this page. Steps: 1 flash balance · 2 E-400 and hot oil · 3 vapour separation · 4 drum diameter, height and hold-up · 5 nozzles · 6 control valves · 7 relief and shell.

        Feed and flash
        E-400 and hot oil
        Drum separation and hold-up
        Hydraulics, valves, relief

        Assumptions and limits of this sizing

        • Thermodynamics are the simulator's: ideal solution (Raoult) with Antoine vapour pressures, liquid enthalpy from constant cp, vapour enthalpy with Watson latent heats, ideal-gas vapour density. No pressure drop in the drum.
        • Souders–Brown Ks values are typical for a vertical drum at low pressure (with a mesh pad about 0.08–0.11 m/s, without about half of that); vendors derate Ks at high pressure, for foaming and for high liquid load.
        • Level alarm and trip positions are the page's own (LIC-400 alarms, LSHH-416, LSLL-417) as fractions of the level span; the vapour space is built from the three heights entered (inlet nozzle, mesh pad, top) — typical minimums, not a standard.
        • The diameter is solved so that the tangent-to-tangent height meets the H/D target (typical 3–5 for a vertical drum), then increased if the vapour needs more area. 2:1 ellipsoidal heads (depth D/4, volume πD³/24, surface ≈ 1.084 D²).
        • E-400 is sized for the entered case (ε-NTU, counter-current). "Existing E-400" rates the simulator's UA at the entered feed with the model's flow correction UA ∝ 1/(½ (ṁ/ṁd)−0.8 + ½ (ṁoil/ṁoil,d)−0.8). U = 300 W/m² K is assumed.
        • Valve openings use the installed capacities of the simulator's valves and an equal-% characteristic; the supply droop and E-400/piping losses scale with the square of the feed mass flow. Nozzle limits are typical: inlet ρv² as entered, vapour outlet ρv² ≤ 3750 Pa, liquid outlet ≤ 1 m/s; sch 40 inside diameters.
        • Relief: two cases only, single-component-like vapour properties at the bubble point, k = 1.1, Z = 1, Kd = 0.975, no back-pressure correction. Shell thickness: t = P R/(S E − 0.6 P) + 3 mm corrosion allowance with an assumed allowable stress S = 138 MPa and joint efficiency E = 0.85 (ASME VIII Div. 1 form); wind, nozzle loads and minimum fabrication thickness ignored. All of these are teaching simplifications, not a substitute for API 520/521 and ASME VIII.

        1 · BFD, PFD and P&ID: three drawings, three jobs

        Each drawing answers a different question. The BFD says what happens to the material, the PFD says with which equipment and at what conditions, the P&ID says exactly how it is built and controlled. They are drawn in that order during a project and read in the reverse order in the field.

        2 · The D-400 block flow diagram

        The Process tab draws the unit as blocks with the key valves and loops, and numbers seven streams. Process streams are ◇1–◇5; the hot-oil utility is ◇6 and ◇7. Stream ◇3 is the only two-phase stream: the feed starts to boil in the let-down valve, not in E-400.

        Copied from the Process tab so the two always match. Blue: process liquid; blue-green dashes: two-phase; green: vapour; red: hot oil. Dashed coloured lines are the four control loops.

        3 · Blocks: what goes in, what comes out, what each does

        Two things never appear as numbered streams on this BFD: the N2 blanket (it flows only when the drum pressure falls to about 30 kPa g, normally zero) and relief through PSV-400 to flare (zero unless the pressure reaches the set point). A balance must still leave room for them.

        4 · Stream table: Design and Now

        Same numbers and formulas as the Process tab stream table. Pressures upstream of FCV-400 (◇1, ◇2) are estimated from the line and exchanger pressure drops, not measured; ◇5 is at the drum bottom (static head included). C4 of ◇1–◇3 is the design feed (no feed analyser); ◇4 and ◇5 are AI-420 and AI-410. Now columns are shaded.

        5 · Boundary balances around the blocks

        Draw a boundary around a block and everything that crosses it must add up: mass in = mass out, each component in = out, heat in = heat out. The model rows use the simulator's own flows; the DCS rows use only what a board operator can see (meters, analysers, temperatures), which is how a real unit is checked. Diff % = (out − in) / in. A row turns red only when its difference moves more than 2 points away from its design value, because some rows are not exactly zero even at design.

        What the DCS cannot close. There is no feed analyser, so every feed composition term is the design 35 wt% (or the last lab sample). There is no flow meter on the hot-oil header or return, only FT-405 on the E-400 branch, so the TCV-401 bypass flow and the heat drawn from the hot-oil system are not known. Relief to flare, the drain and the N2 blanket flow have no meters either; the drum heat loss is not measured. Where a balance cannot be closed from meters, the gap is found by difference and confirmed in the field.
        Why a closed balance at design can still show a gap
        • Accumulation. At steady state in = out. While the level or pressure is still moving, the difference is what is stored in (or drawn from) D-400: an open mass row on a lined-out plant means a stream is leaving by a path with no meter.
        • Measurement basis. Volume meters need a density; an analyser reads with a lag; a vapour meter counts N2 and entrained liquid as vapour. The DCS rows carry these errors, the model rows do not.
        • Transport delay. TI-401 sits after E-400 and a length of pipe: for a few minutes after a change the feed-side duty lags the hot-oil side.
        • Terms left out. The metered flash balance ignores the small heat loss of the drum (about 0.5 % at design); that is its design gap.

        6 · From BFD to PFD

        The PFD keeps the same boundaries and stream directions but replaces each block with real equipment and adds what is needed to size and cost it:

        • the feed supply pump P-400 appears as the source of the feed pressure; E-400 becomes a shell-and-tube symbol with the hot oil on one side and the feed on the other;
        • the drum gets its mesh pad, nozzles and relief line to flare, and the N2 blanket appears as a utility stream;
        • control valves FCV-400, TCV-401, PCV-420, LCV-400 and PCV-430 are drawn on the lines they act on;
        • streams are renumbered in drawing order (the PFD's own numbers, shown with the BFD number in brackets on the PFD tab) and carry flags of mass flow, temperature and pressure;
        • an equipment list and design basis are added in the title block.

        • Real equipment with tags and standard symbols (ISO 10628): the feed pump P-400, the shell-and-tube E-400, the vertical drum D-400 with its mesh pad.

          1 · Operability and the operating window

          Process operability means the plant has the capacity and flexibility to reach a range of operating conditions safely, reliably and profitably, with good dynamic performance and product quality. The operating window is the range of achievable steady-state operation: every controlled variable held at its set point and no limit crossed. Four things shape it.

          The variables of D-400

          ClassVariable (tag)DesignWhy it is in this class

          2 · Variability: the design basis the window must cover

          "The abnormal is normal." A window is only as good as the list of changes it was sized for. The five sources of variability, written as a design-basis memorandum for D-400. The model column comes from one-at-a-time steady-state runs of this simulator (all loops in automatic, design set points); ranges are teaching values unless an alarm or the model's own disturbance range sets them.

          SourceWhat changes on D-400Range used hereHow oftenWhat the model saysCovered by

          A single human error must not cause an unsafe condition or environmental damage and must not stay undetected. That is why every bound in part 3 has an alarm and the fast, damaging ones (level high-high, level low-low, pressure high-high) have a trip.

          3 · Bounds and the integrity operating window

          The bounds frame the window: upper and lower limits set by materials, equipment, safety and product quality. A hard bound cannot be crossed without damage or hazard (liquid into the vapour line, gas blow-by into the liquid line, overpressure, boiling inside E-400); a capacity bound is a handle at the end of its travel; a spec bound is product quality; a soft bound (alarm) can be crossed for a while. The table shows the design value, the live value and how much of the design margin is left.

          BoundKindWhy it existsLimitDesignNowMargin now ÷ margin at design

          Reading the integrity operating window (IOW). Inside the target range the drum is stable and the products are on specification. Between the target and the standard limit (the alarm) the unit is still safe but time counts: the operator must act. Past the critical limit damage or loss of containment follows quickly, so the SIS acts there (Safety system tab). Level and pressure are the two IOW variables of a flash drum; the hot-feed temperature is a third, because above it the feed starts to boil inside E-400 and the let-down valve.

          4 · Design for the worst case, and a live point check

          Equipment is sized for the worst case of the variability it must handle, and each piece has its own. For E-400 (Q = UA·F·ΔTlm) it is the highest feed, the coldest feed, the coolest hot oil and the most fouling; for the let-down valve it is the highest feed with the lowest supply pressure and the hottest, lightest feed; for PCV-420 the most vapour against the highest header pressure. Pick a case or set your own point: the page runs a copy of this model to steady state (all loops in automatic, trips off, 3000 s of plant time) and checks every bound.

          5 · Capacity and turndown

          A small plant that only just meets the design point is cheap but has no window; a large one has a window but costs capital and may run poorly at low rate. The capacity must be safe, protect the equipment and meet quality for the base case and frequently occurring variability; lower production is acceptable in rare cases; stop for extreme ones. Turndown ratio = normal maximum ÷ normal minimum, where "normal" means sustainable without hazard or damage.

          Each element has its own feed range; the unit's range is the overlap, so it is always narrower than any single element's. Ranges below come from feed sweeps on the model (3–26 m³/h, 35 wt% feed, 10 °C, set points as chosen), interpolated between the 1 m³/h grid points.

          ElementTurndown, rangeability or capacity on D-400TypicalFlexibility

          7 · Type II: the set points each disturbance needs, and the spec window

          Now TIC-401 and PIC-420 are in automatic and hold their set points, and FIC-400 and LIC-400 hold feed and level.           8 · Type III: the disturbances D-400 can absorb

          Type III keeps the handles inside their ranges and asks which disturbances can be corrected. Here the disturbances are feed rate and feed composition (the two that matter most), with the hot-oil supply temperature as a selector; the set points are either the design ones or the wider-margin pair found in part 7. Each cell is one steady state coloured by the bound that fails first (root cause first).

          9 · Monte Carlo operating window

          The recipe: (1) simulate the base case, (2) replace the uncertain inputs by samples from their distributions and repeat, (3) mark each sample feasible or infeasible against every bound, (4) report the fraction and show it. Here 1000 samples of feed rate (normal), feed composition (normal) and hot-oil supply (uniform) are interpolated (trilinear, on the smallest bound margin) in the part 8 grids, which were run on the model; a sample outside the grid (feed below 6 or above 24 m³/h, butane outside 29–41 wt%) is counted as outside the window.

          With n adjustable handles and m variables to hold: n = m gives a finite window with each point exactly specified; n < m gives no window (at best the design point) and is not an acceptable design; n > m leaves extra freedom that can be used to optimise.

            The Operating windows tab finds where D-400 can run; this tab looks at the handles that move it there. Gains, spare capacities and responses come from runs on copies of this simulator's model (all loops AUTO unless stated, trips off so limits show as numbers). The valve and exchanger curves in parts 4 and 5 evaluate the model's own hydraulic and E-400 relations at the design state: an illustration calibrated to this page, checked against the model runs.

            1 What flexibility is · 2 How many · 3 Where · 4 Fluid flow · 5 Heat transfer · 6 Production rate · 7 Strategies · 8 How much · 9 Recommendations

            1 · What flexibility is

            Flexibility is the ability of a plant to run reliably over a range of rates, feeds and conditions without losing quantity or quality. It is what lets us steer the process after the equipment has been built: reach new set points and cancel disturbances.

            Without it D-400 passes every hot-oil, feed and header disturbance straight on to the product compositions, the level and the pressure. With it the four control valves absorb them, as long as each has travel left.

            How it is provided

            • Spare capacity: valve travel above the design opening, exchanger area, supply pressure.
            • Adjustable utility flows: hot oil to E-400, N₂ blanket.
            • By-passes: the 3-way TCV-401 sends part of the hot oil around E-400; globe by-passes around each control valve.

            Four design questions: how many handles, where, which tools, and how much capacity.

            The flexibility register of D-400

            HandleWhat it adjustsKind of flexibilityAt designSpare at designStatus

            2 · How many handles? Degrees of freedom

            A design is controllable only if the number of adjustable handles n ≥ the number of variables to be held m. The degrees of freedom set the most variables we can hold; the variables we insist on set the fewest handles we need.

            Variable D-400 must holdWhyHandle usedSteady-state effect?

            n = m = 4: FCV-400, TCV-401, LCV-400 and PCV-420 for feed, hot-feed temperature, level and pressure. But only three of them move the steady state: the level is an inventory with no steady-state effect on the products.

            So D-400 has one rate handle and two quality handles (temperature and pressure) for its two product specifications, AI-420 ≥ 75 wt% and AI-410 ≤ 28 wt%. Asking also for a fixed vapour rate makes m = 3 with n = 2 for quality: one of the three must float. The manual by-passes and the N₂ regulator add no steady-state degree of freedom in normal operation.

            3 · Where? Causal paths from each handle

            Each held variable needs a handle with an independent causal path to it. Interaction is allowed as long as every desired point can still be reached. Three cases:

            Steady-state gains from the model

            +5 % on the valve output with TIC-401 and PIC-420 in manual (FIC-400 and LIC-400 in AUTO), and set-point moves with all loops in AUTO. Highlighted cells are large effects.

            Reaching both product specifications: a 2 × 2 inverse

            Ask for a change in the two compositions; the page solves the linear model of the TIC-401 and PIC-420 set points (closed-loop set-point gains from model runs) for the moves, then lets you check the answer on a copy of the model.

            4 · Flexibility for fluid flow

            For a liquid the flow settles where the driving pressure equals the losses: ṁ = √(ΔP / (Σk + 1/(ρCv²))). Only the valve term is adjustable, so a valve's flexibility is the pressure it is allowed to take. D-400 has three flows with three kinds of driving force.

            4a · Feed: supply curve, E-400 and line losses, FCV-400

            Illustration calibrated to the model's own relations (step() in model.js; checked against owRun to 0.1 %): supply 650 kPa g shut-off minus ksṁ² (≈ 600 at design), E-400 40 kPa and line 10 kPa at design flow, FCV-400 equal-percentage (R = 30) sized for 73.5 % at design, HV-403 Cv = 0.35 × FCV-400 wide open. The drum pressure is held at the PIC-420 set point. The FCV-400 inlet must stay above the hot feed's bubble pressure: that is why the let-down valve sits after E-400 and why the supply pressure is itself a capacity.

            6 · Flexibility for production rate

            At steady state material and energy must balance in the unit. One flexible variable sets the rate; every other flow follows automatically, without people, and two measured flows are never simply matched (meter errors would accumulate in the drum). Level and pressure show the inventories.

            HAZID · Hazard identification of the D-400 flash drum unit

            A plant-level, checklist-driven identification of the major hazards around the flash drum, done before (and wider than) the detailed HAZOP. It uses an example 5 × 5 risk matrix for teaching; a real study uses the owner's matrix and a multidisciplinary team.

            Teaching slide deck (28 slides, interactive) — what HAZID is and how to run it, the D-400 PFD areas and guidewords, the hazard register, risk matrix, major accident hazards and follow-up studies.
            Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

            1 What HAZID is · 2 Method · 3 PFD and study areas · 4 Guideword checklist · 5 Hazard register · 6 Major accident hazards · 7 From HAZID to HAZOP

            1 · What HAZID is and where it sits

            HAZID (hazard identification) is a structured brainstorm of what could go badly wrong across the whole facility, its surroundings, people and environment. It is done early — concept and front-end design — with the PFD, the plot plan and the design basis, so that major hazards shape the design before the details are fixed. It asks broad questions ("what hazards exist here?"); HAZOP asks detailed ones ("what if there is no flow in this line?").

            HAZIDHAZOP
            WhenConcept / FEED, and before major changesDetailed design with the P&ID frozen; periodic revalidation
            DrawingPFD, plot plan, design basisP&ID, cause-and-effect chart, operating procedures
            BreakdownAreas or systems (A1–A7 here)Nodes with one design intent (N1–N7 here)
            PromptGuideword checklist by hazard category (natural, external, process, utilities, health, occupational, environment, operations, organisation)Guide word × parameter (NO flow, MORE pressure, LESS level …)
            ScopeProcess and non-process hazards, site and surroundingsProcess deviations and operability problems
            OutputHazard register, list of major accident hazards (MAH), studies to do next (HAZOP, fire and explosion, SIL, layout, relief)Worksheets and recommendations per deviation
            ReferenceISO 17776 (major accident hazard management in design, with HAZID and its checklist); company HSE practiceIEC 61882

            For D-400 the HAZID must answer questions the P&ID alone cannot: is a 10 m³ drum of LPG-range liquid acceptable next to a hot-oil exchanger, where does the relief go, what fire could reach the drum, and who can be hurt by nitrogen, hot oil or hexane.

            2 · Method

            1. Define scope and basis: D-400 from the feed battery limit (supply from tankage, P-400) through FT-400, E-400 and the FCV-400 let-down, to the vapour product at the fuel-gas header and the liquid product at the downstream unit; the hot-oil, N2, instrument-air and power supplies; site conditions; the risk matrix below.
            2. Divide the plant into areas on the PFD (section 3).
            3. Apply the guideword checklist to each area (section 4): for every category ask whether the hazard exists here, what could release it (cause or threat) and what would follow (top event and outcome).
            4. Record the existing controls, split into prevention (stops the top event) and mitigation (limits the outcome), as in a bow-tie.
            5. Rank the risk and flag the major accident hazards: events that could cause a fatality or several, major damage or a major environmental release.
            6. Assign actions and further studies: design changes, HAZOP nodes, relief and flare, fire and explosion, SIL, layout, permits.

            Risk matrix (teaching example). Severity S is judged on the worst credible consequence with no credit for safeguards; likelihood L is judged with the existing safeguards in place. R = S × L.

              7 · From HAZID to HAZOP and other studies

              • Trips that protect against MAHs — I-1 (LSHH-416, PSHH-426) and I-2 (LSLL-417) — go to a SIL assessment and LOPA (IEC 61511); see the Safety layers and LOPA tabs.
              • Fire hazards (HZ-01, HZ-05, HZ-09, HZ-11, HZ-15, HZ-17, HZ-23) go to a fire and explosion analysis, gas-detection mapping and a layout / separation-distance check.
              • Relief cases (HZ-04, HZ-06, HZ-10, HZ-11, HZ-16) go to a relief and flare study (API 520 / 521).
              • Occupational and health hazards (HZ-18, HZ-24 to HZ-26) go to the permit-to-work, confined-space and PPE procedures.
              • The same scenario carries the same rank in the HAZOP tab worksheets (for example D-400 overpressure, gas blow-by, external fire and air in the drum S5 × L2; carry-over and blocked-in E-400 S4 × L3), and each action names the HAZOP recommendation (R-…) that takes it further.
              • The register is revisited whenever the design or the feed changes (management of change).

              4 · Degrees of freedom (DOF)

              Why it matters. The degrees of freedom say how many variables can be held at chosen values. Try to control more CVs than there are independent handles and the controllers fight over one valve; control fewer and some variable drifts wherever the disturbances push it.

              NDOF = Nvariables − Nindependent equations = Ndisturbances (fixed by the surroundings) + Nmanipulated

              For control the useful count is the control DOF = the number of independent handles, here the valves.

              4.1 Steady-state count for D-400

              Variables (15)Independent equations (11)
              F feed flow
              Th hot-feed temperature
              Q E-400 duty
              W hot-oil flow through E-400
              P drum pressure
              T flash temperature
              V vapour flow
              L liquid flow
              y, x vapour and liquid C4 fraction (2)
              h level
              uF, uT, uL, uP positions of FCV-400, TCV-401, LCV-400, PCV-420 (4)              		 1 Feed hydraulics: F = f(uF, supply pressure, P)
              2 Hot-oil hydraulics: W = f(uT, header ΔP)
              3 E-400 transfer: Q = f(F, W, feed and oil temperatures)
              4 E-400 feed side: Q = F cp(Th − Tin)
              5 Total balance: F = V + L
              6 C4 balance: F z = V y + L x
              7 Adiabatic flash: F hF(Th) = V H(y, T) + L h(x, T)
              8, 9 Equilibrium (Raoult) for C4 and C6 at T, P
              10 Vapour valve: V = f(uP, P, header pressure)
              11 Liquid valve: L = f(uL, P + static head of h, receiver pressure)

              DOF = 15 − 11 = 4, exactly the four control valves FCV-400, TCV-401, LCV-400, PCV-420. Feed composition and temperature, supply pressure, oil temperature, header and receiver pressures are disturbances, not counted. Each hand valve (HV-403, HV-413, HV-423 bypasses, HV-430) adds one more DOF, but the procedure fixes them (bypasses shut, N2 isolation open), so they are not used for control. The trip valves XV-408, XV-409 and XV-418 are on/off and belong to the SIS, not to control.

              4.2 The level has no steady-state effect

              The level h appears only in equation 11, through a small static head. Hold F, Th and P and the products do not care where the level sits. So one DOF (LCV-400) must be spent on the inventory — without it the level integrates away — and the level set point is a free choice that moves no steady-state product. The steady-state operating DOF is 4 − 1 = 3: feed rate, hot-feed temperature and drum pressure. Checked on the model (other loops in AUTO):

              Running on a copy of the model …

              4.3 How each DOF is used

              DOF (handle)Used to fixByWhy this use
              FCV-400FFIC-400 (AUTO)Production sets the rate; the valve acts directly and in seconds on the flow.
              TCV-401Th (Rev B: W inside, Th outside)TIC-401 (AUTO or CAS master of FIC-405)Hot oil is the only handle on the heat; one sign, about a minute.
              LCV-400h (Rev B: L inside, h outside)LIC-400 (AUTO or CAS master of FIC-410)The inventory must be held; the liquid valve has the direct effect.
              PCV-420PPIC-420 (AUTO)The vapour valve moves the pressure within seconds.
              Hand valvestheir own positionsOperator, by procedureIsolation, bypass for maintenance, N2 blanket.

              With F, Th and P held, the product compositions are fixed for a given feed; that is why no composition controller is needed at normal operation (section 6).

              4.4 DOF of each loop

              • A feedback loop uses one DOF: it turns "valve position is free" into "CV = SP". The SP becomes the new free input, given by the operator or a master controller.
              • Cascade adds no DOF. In Rev B, TIC-401 → FIC-405 and LIC-400 → FIC-410 still act through TCV-401 and LCV-400. The same is true of ratio, feedforward and trim: one valve, one DOF, used better.
              • A loop in MAN gives its DOF back to the operator. A valve at 0 % or 100 % loses its DOF: the controller asks for more than the valve can give and the CV is then uncontrolled, whatever the tuning.
              • Two controllers must never move one valve at the same time, unless a selector or a split range decides which one acts (section 7).

              TIC-401 → FIC-405 (Rev B)TCV-4011 (same)Hot-feed SPas above, or FIC-405 not in CAS

              5 · The control loops on the P&ID

              The tuning column is read from the running simulator, so a change made on a DCS faceplate shows here.

              6 · How the loops were chosen

              1. Start from the objectives and the DOF. Four valves, so at most four automatic loops; the level must take one of them, leaving feed rate, heat and pressure as the three operating handles.
              2. Pair each CV with the MV that moves it most directly, fastest and with one sign. The open-loop test below steps each valve with every loop in MAN: pressure → vapour valve, level → liquid valve, temperature → hot oil, flow → let-down valve are the strong, fast, one-signed entries.
              3. Measure the flow where it is single-phase and cold (FT-400 before E-400) and let down after heating, so E-400 stays liquid; the flow loop also removes supply-pressure changes within seconds.
              4. Keep safety separate from control. LSHH-416, LSLL-417 and PSHH-426 have their own sensors; a failed LT-400 or PT-420 cannot disable its trip, and a trip does not depend on the controller being in AUTO.
              5. Choose fail positions for the safe state, independent of controller action: feed and liquid valves close, the vapour valve opens, the hot oil goes to bypass.
              6. Do not control composition directly at the drum. The analysers lag (first-order 30–40 s in the model; real analysers add a sample cycle of minutes, typical), the liquid holdup of about min mixes every change slowly, and temperature and pressure each move both compositions, so two composition loops would interact (table below). Temperature and pressure are fast, reliable stand-ins; the operator moves their set points when AI-420 or AI-410 drift.
              7. Use the drum as a surge volume. The level loop is tuned for averaging: the level may move within its band so the liquid to the downstream unit changes slowly.
              8. Put a fast inner flow loop under a slow loop when a disturbance enters through the valve path (Rev B: hot-oil header ΔP for TIC-401, receiver pressure for LIC-400).

              Running on a copy of the model …

              Shaded cells are the pairings used. Level slope is the change per minute between 1 and 5 minutes after the step.

              6.2 Pairing test

              6.3 Why temperature and pressure, not composition

              Running on a copy of the model …

              With temperature and pressure held, a feed-rate change leaves both compositions where they were: the flash depends on T, P and the feed composition, not on the rate. Feed composition is the one common disturbance that holding T and P does not reject; the analysers are alarmed so the operator knows when a set point must move.

              7 · Loop structures and their principles

              StructurePrincipleUse it whenOn D-400
              Manual (open loop)The operator sets the valve; nothing corrects disturbances.The handle changes rarely or is fixed by procedure.Globe bypasses, N2 isolation, drain, block valves
              Single feedbackMeasure the CV, compare with SP, move the MV to remove the error. Corrects any disturbance, but only after it has moved the CV.Almost always the base layer.FIC-400, TIC-401, LIC-400, PIC-420 (Rev A)
              CascadeThe master sets the SP of a faster slave on the MV path; the slave removes its own disturbances first. Slave 3–5 times faster; tune it first.A disturbance enters through the valve path.Rev B: TIC-401 → FIC-405 (header ΔP), LIC-400 → FIC-410 (receiver pressure)
              RatioOne flow's SP = ratio × another (wild) flow.A proportion must be kept without waiting for a quality signal.Not used. A hot-oil : feed ratio on FIC-405 with TIC-401 trimming the ratio would be the ratio form of the feedforward below.
              FeedforwardMeasure a disturbance and move the MV before the CV changes, from a model of its effect.
