              Override / selectorTwo controllers share one valve through a low or high selector; the one nearer its limit takes over; the other must have anti-windup.A constraint must be protected while another CV is normally controlled.Proposed: low-level override — a tight LIC-401 (SP 20 %) and the averaging LIC-400 through a low selector on LCV-400; high-pressure override — a tight PIC-421 (SP 130 kPa g) through a high selector on PCV-420 when PIC-420 is tuned smooth for the header.
              Split rangeOne controller output drives two valves in sequence.One CV needs two handles that act in opposite directions.Proposed: PIC-420 OUT 0–50 % closes an N2 make-up valve, 50–100 % opens PCV-420, so pressure is held at low vapour rates (start-up, low feed) instead of relying on the separate PCV-430.
              Safety instrumented functionsDiscrete logic on independent sensors drives the unit to the safe state. Not a control loop; not bypassed by the operator.Hazards that control cannot be trusted with.I-1 (LSHH-416, PSHH-426 → XV-408, XV-409), I-2 (LSLL-417 → XV-418), ESD

              8 · P, PI and PID on D-400

              Every controller in the simulator uses the ideal form in % of span, derivative on the PV (no kick on SP changes) and an anti-windup clamp: OUT = Kc[e + (1/Ti)∫e dt − Td dPV/dt] + bias. What each term does, offset, windup and the tuning rules are explained in the Control basics tab. Here: which mode each D-400 loop needs, and its tuning from a step test on the model.

              8.1 Guidance by loop type

              Loop type on D-400ModeGainResetDerivativeWhy
              Liquid flow: FIC-400, FIC-405, FIC-410PIlow (0.3–0.5)short (2–4 s)noneFast, noisy; the valve lag is the process. High gain makes the valve chatter.
              Exchanger outlet temperature: TIC-401PI (PID optional)moderate≈ τ (about a minute)small, optionalDead time from transport through E-400; derivative helps a little on load steps.
              Averaging level: LIC-400PI (P alone leaves an offset after a load change)lowlong (≈ 2 × arrest time)noneIntegrating process; the level is meant to move so the outflow changes slowly. Keep Kc·Ti large to avoid slow cycling.
              Gas pressure: PIC-420PIhighminutesnoneFast vapour-space response plus a slow part from the boiling liquid.
              Composition (AI-420, AI-410), if ever closedPI, slow, as a trim on the TIC-401 or PIC-420 SPlowlongnoneAnalyser lag and interaction (section 6).

              8.2 Step tests on the model and suggested tuning

              Loop in MAN, OUT stepped +5 %, PV recorded. Self-regulating loops: K = ΔPV/ΔOUT in % of span, τ = 1.5(t63 − t28), θ = t63 − τ, lambda PI Kc = τ/[|K|(λ + θ)], Ti = τ. Integrating level: K* = slope / ΔOUT, Kc = (2λ + θ)/[|K*|(λ + θ)²], Ti = 2λ + θ with λ the arrest time.

              Choose a loop and a test, set the mode and tuning, then Run. Each run starts a copy of the model at design (noise off) and applies the test after 5 % of the run; the dashed grey line is the simulator's own tuning on the same test. The running session is not touched. For graded exercises on the live unit see the Tuning lab tab.

              Loop and test
              Controller
              Presets

              Things to try (numbers from runs of this lab)

              1. TIC-401, load: feed 16 → 18 m³/h. P only leaves the hot feed about 2.3 °C low for good; the simulator PI dips 2.0 °C and is back within ±0.3 °C in about 4 minutes, with no offset.
              2. Same test, "with feedforward". The dip shrinks from 2.0 °C to about 0.2 °C: TCV-401 opens as soon as FT-400 moves, before the colder feed reaches TT-401. Feedback still removes what the feedforward gain gets wrong.
              3. TIC-401, load: hot-oil header ΔP 150 → 105 kPa. Rev A dips 2.4 °C; switch Structure to Rev B and the dip is about 0.6 °C, because FIC-405 restores the oil flow within seconds. On the feed step Rev B gains nothing: that disturbance does not pass through the valve path.
              4. TIC-401, SP step 74 → 76 °C. Shorten Ti from 55 to 30 and 15 s: overshoot grows from none to about 0.15 and 0.7 °C. The tight preset (Kc ≈ 2.8) settles in under a minute with about 0.1 °C overshoot. On the feed step, PID with Td = 20 s trims the dip only from 2.0 to 1.8 °C: dead time is small against τ.
              5. LIC-400, load: feed 16 → 18 m³/h. P only settles about 2.6 % above SP; PI returns to SP. On an SP step P only ends close to the new SP: an integrating process needs no integral for set-point changes, only for loads.
              6. LIC-400, tight preset (arrest 3 min). The feed-step peak falls from 1.8 % (simulator tuning) to 0.6 %, but on the SP step LCV-400 swings down to about 10 %: every level move is passed to the downstream unit. That is why D-400 uses averaging.
              7. PIC-420, load: vapour header 30 → 60 kPa g. P only leaves about 4 kPa offset; the simulator PI peaks 2.6 kPa; Kc = 12 cuts the peak to about 1.2 kPa at the cost of a busier PCV-420 and a harder push on the header.
              8. FIC-400, SP step, Kc 2, Ti 1 s. The flow overshoots by about 44 % of the step and OUT swings from 72 to 84 %: fast loops want modest gain and a reset near the valve time constant.

              HAZOP · Hazard and Operability Study of D-400

              Teaching slide deck (30 slides, interactive) — what HAZOP is and how it runs, the D-400 nodes, guide words and worksheet, risk ranking, recommendations and the dynamic check on the model.
              Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

              A teaching HAZOP of the flash drum as drawn on the P&ID tab, done node by node with the IEC 61882 guide words. Risk ranking uses the example matrix of part 5; a real study uses the owner's corporate matrix, a multidisciplinary team and the as-built documents. Design values in the text are computed from the lined-out model; alarm and trip limits come from the alarm table and the SIS settings of this page.

              1 Standard and method · 2 Team and documents · 3 Nodes · 4 Guide words and parameters · 5 Risk matrix · 6 Worksheets · 7 Coverage check · 8 Recommendations · 9 Dynamic check on the simulator · 10 Follow-up and close-out

              1 · Standard and method (IEC 61882)

              HAZOP is a structured, team-based examination of a defined system. Each part of the design is compared with its design intent; guide words combined with process parameters generate deviations; for each credible deviation the team records causes, consequences, existing safeguards and, where the risk is not acceptable, recommendations. It finds hazards (harm to people, environment, assets) and operability problems (the unit cannot make on-spec product or cannot be run as intended).

              ReferenceWhat it contributes to this study
              IEC 61882:2016 Hazard and operability studies (HAZOP studies) – Application guideDefinitions, the four phases, the guide words, team roles, recording
              CCPS Guidelines for Hazard Evaluation ProceduresWorksheet format, node selection, consequences judged without safeguards, risk ranking, hand-over to LOPA
              IEC 61511 (functional safety, SIS)How HAZOP scenarios that rely on SIS I-1 and I-2 go to LOPA to set the required SIL of LSHH-416, LSLL-417 and PSHH-426 loops
              ISO 31000 and the owner's risk matrixRisk criteria used to decide whether the safeguards are adequate
              API 520 / API 521Relief sizing and the relief cases for PSV-400 (blocked outlet, external fire, control-valve failure, regulator failure), depressuring, flare loads
              ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section VIIID-400 design pressure (MAWP), design temperature, minimum design metal temperature, overpressure protection
              Thailand: Department of Industrial Works regulation on hazard identification, risk assessment and risk-management plans (B.E. 2543)Legal duty to identify hazards (HAZOP is an accepted method) and to prepare a risk-management plan for the factory
              OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 (PSM), where applicableProcess hazard analysis for a covered process (flammable liquids and gases), revalidated at least every five years

              The four phases

              1. Definition: scope, objectives, team and risk matrix. Scope here: from the feed battery limit (upstream of XV-408) through E-400 (both sides, from XV-409), D-400 with PSV-400 and the N2 blanket, to the vapour battery limit (downstream of HV-421) and the liquid battery limit (downstream of HV-411). Excluded: the supply tankage and pump, the hot-oil heater, the fuel-gas header, the flare and the downstream unit (their interfaces are recorded as causes and consequences).
              2. Preparation: collect the P&ID (both sheets), the stream table and design limits, the SIS cause-and-effect chart, the alarm list, the procedures; divide the unit into nodes; write each design intent; choose parameters and guide words.
              3. Examination: for each node → state the design intent → choose a parameter → apply each guide word → is the deviation meaningful? → causes → consequences assuming the safeguards fail → existing safeguards → rank the risk → recommend → next guide word. Every meaningful deviation is recorded, including those with adequate safeguards (full recording), so the reasoning can be audited later.
              4. Documentation and follow-up: worksheets, recommendation register with owners and dates, close-out, and revalidation after changes (MOC) and periodically.

              Consequences are judged with no credit for safeguards (the worst credible outcome if every safeguard failed); the likelihood L is then judged with the existing safeguards working as designed. Keeping the two apart stops a safeguard being counted twice.

              2 · Team and documents

              RoleResponsibility in this study
              HAZOP leader (chair)Independent of the design; runs the method, keeps the team on the node, decides when a deviation is covered
              Scribe (recorder)Writes the worksheet live and reads back each recommendation
              Process engineer (designer)Design intent, balances, bubble-point margins, relief cases
              Operations representativeHow D-400 is really run: start-up with N2 sweep, rounds, draining, tank switches
              Instrument / control engineerLoops, fail positions (FC/FO), SIS logic, independence of LSHH-416, LSLL-417, PSHH-426
              Safety / risk engineerRisk matrix, LOPA follow-up, regulations
              Specialists as neededMechanical (E-400, vessel ratings), utilities (hot oil, N2, instrument air), downstream and header owners

              Study documents are the tabs of this simulator: P&ID (sheet 1 process, sheet 2 loop data and SIS cause-and-effect), Process (stream table, unit conditions, pressure profile), Design of the unit operation (limits and sizing), Control loop design (loops, fail positions), Safety system (SIS) (trip logic and resets), Workbook (alarm and trip list) and the start-up, shutdown and emergency procedures in the Exercises tab. The HAZID tab covers the site-level hazards; the Safety layers and LOPA tabs take this study further.

              3 · Nodes

              A node is a section of the plant with one clear design intent. Boundaries sit where the intent changes: the let-down valve drops the pressure, the exchanger heats, the drum separates, each product line delivers to its own receiver. The hot-oil side of E-400 is its own node because its intent (deliver heat) differs from the feed side (be heated and stay liquid). Procedures get a node because start-up, shutdown, draining and maintenance create deviations that steady operation does not. Click a node box to open its worksheet.

              4 · Guide words and parameters

              A deviation is recorded only when it is physically meaningful ("REVERSE temperature" is not). Guide words may also be combined with a parameter in plain words ("less level", "no flow", "hot oil as well as feed").

              5 · Risk matrix (example for teaching)

              Number in brackets: deviations of this study in the cell. Risk R = S × L.

              SSeverity (worst credible consequence, no credit for safeguards)
              1No injury; minor upset; no release
              2First aid; off-spec product; short outage; small contained release
              3Lost-time injury; unit down for days; local release or small fire
              4Single fatality or permanent disability; major equipment damage; fire in the unit
              5Multiple fatalities; vessel rupture or explosion; fire or release beyond the unit
              LLikelihood with the existing safeguards
              1Remote: < 10⁻⁴ /yr
              2Unlikely: 10⁻⁴–10⁻³ /yr
              3Possible in the plant life: 10⁻³–10⁻² /yr
              4Likely, several times in the plant life: 10⁻²–10⁻¹ /yr
              5Frequent: > 10⁻¹ /yr

              1–4 Low acceptable · 5–9 Medium reduce if practicable (ALARP), review the safeguards · 10–16 High recommendation required, take to LOPA · 20–25 Very high not acceptable, act before operation

              6 · HAZOP worksheets (node by node)

              Consequences are written assuming the safeguards fail. S ranks that consequence; L ranks its likelihood with the listed safeguards working. Causes include the simulator's fault library, written as engineering causes.

              7 · Coverage check: guide words applied in each node

              Numbers: rows recorded. A dot: the guide word was considered and gave no meaningful deviation in that node. EARLY, LATE, BEFORE and AFTER apply mainly to the procedure node N7. The second table checks that every node has flow, pressure and temperature (or their equivalents) covered.

              8 · Recommendation register

              9 · Dynamic check of selected deviations on the simulator

              A conventional HAZOP judges consequences by experience. Here selected deviations are run on a copy of the D-400 model, starting from the lined-out design state, with the existing safeguards active (alarms from the alarm table evaluated every second, SIS I-1 and I-2 armed, PSV-400, controllers in their normal modes) and no operator action, for up to 30 min or until SIS I-1 trips. The live simulator is not touched. The runs show whether the safeguards act before harm and how much time the operator has.

              Ten runs of up to 30 simulated minutes each; a few seconds in total.
              Press the button to run the checks.

              What the runs tell the HAZOP team

              • Appears after the runs.

              10 · Follow-up and close-out

              • Each recommendation gets an owner and a due date; the owner answers accepted and done, accepted with an alternative (with justification) or rejected (with a justification agreed by the HAZOP leader and the plant manager). The register in part 8 is the tracking list.
              • High and very-high rows whose protection relies on SIS I-1 or I-2 (high level, gas blow-by, high pressure) go to LOPA to confirm the required SIL (IEC 61511); see the LOPA tab.
              • Relief cases raised here (blocked outlet, external fire, TCV-401 failed to E-400, PCV-430 failed open) are closed in the relief study to API 520/521.
              • Any change (putting the Rev B cascades in service, new feeds, a changed alarm limit) goes through management of change, which asks whether the HAZOP must be updated.
              • Revalidate the study periodically (typically every five years) and after incidents or significant changes.
              • Use the simulator to train operators on the scenarios found here and to check that alarm responses and procedures work.

              Safety layers · layers of protection for D-400

              Teaching slide deck (29 slides, interactive) — why protection comes in layers, what the BPCS, alarms and SIS add to the D-400 P&ID (fail positions, alarm deadband, cause and effect, voting), and relief, containment and emergency response.
              Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

              Safety must cover failures of equipment (including control) and of people, and more than one failure at a time, while keeping production where it can. So protection is built in layers, each independent of the others, with more strength held in reserve as an event gets more serious. This tab applies the six-layer hierarchy to the flash drum as drawn on the P&ID tab. Set points, alarm limits and trip settings are read from the model and the alarm table of this page; values marked "assumed" are for teaching, and every recommended addition traces to a HAZOP recommendation (R-xx) or a HAZID action (H-Axx).

              1 The six layers · 2 P&ID layer by layer · 3 What each layer does · 4 Integrity operating window · 5 Independence check · 6 Good practices · 7 Standards

              1 · The six layers

              LayerJobAutomatic?Needs power / computer?Needs a person?
              1 BPCSClosed-loop control keeps D-400 in its operating regionYesYes (DCS, instrument air)Supervises
              2 AlarmsBring an unusual situation to the attention of a personNo actionYesYes: decides
              3 SISStop part of the process: feed and hot oil (I-1), bottoms (I-2)YesYes, but de-energise to tripNo (reset only)
              4 ReliefPrevent excessive (or too low) pressure; divert material safelyYes, self-actuatingNoNo
              5 ContainmentKeep released material from workers, community, environmentPassive or remoteMostly noPartly
              6 Emergency responseEvacuation, fire fighting, health careNoPartlyYes

              Layers 1–3 all need electrical power, computing and communication (and here instrument air), so one power or air failure could take out all three at once. That is why the SIS valves XV-408, XV-409 and XV-418 close with no power and no air, why the control valves fail to their safe side, and why relief, containment and emergency response are kept in reserve. Click a ring to open that layer on the P&ID.

              • IEC 61511 / ISA-84: SIS life cycle, independence, SIL, proof testing, bypass management. CCPS Layer of Protection Analysis and Guidelines for Safe Automation of Chemical Processes.

              The HAZOP tab says what can go wrong on D-400; this tab asks how often, and whether the safeguards are reliable enough.               Part A · Reliability for safety

              A1 · Definitions

              TermMeaningOn D-400
              HazardAn inherent physical or chemical characteristic that can harm people, the environment or propertyFlashing C4/C6 liquid under pressure in D-400 ( kg at 50 % level); hot oil at 180 °C in E-400

              Failure rate λFailures per unit time among the units still workingLT-400 about 1.7 /yr (generic, all modes); the SIS level sensor LSHH-416 0.015 /yr (dangerous undetected, assumed)
              Reliability R(t)Probability of working without failure through an intervalLSHH-416 still able to trip at the end of a one-year test interval

              MTTFMean time to failure = ∫R dt = 1/λ for a constant rateLT-400 about 0.6 yr; the LSHH-416 sensor about 67 yr
              Proof testA test that finds hidden (undetected) failures and restores the device to "as new"Raising the level to LSHH-416 and seeing XV-408 close (HAZOP R-28)
              SIL / RRFSafety integrity level: a PFD band; risk reduction factor RRF = 1/PFDSIF-2 PSHH-426 → XV-408/XV-409 about SIL 2 (A4)
              Initiating event, enabling condition, conditional modifierThe cause that starts the scenario; a condition that must also hold; probabilities of ignition, presence, harmLCV-400 fails closed; the feed over-heated at the same time; people near the drum 10 % of the time
              Deterministic / probabilistic analysisCan the design hold the worst case? / What is the numerical risk and is it tolerable?PSV-400 sized for every relief case (HAZOP R-14) / LOPA in Part B

              Is 99.9 % reliability good enough? A one-in-a-thousand failure a year would mean an unsafe landing every day at a busy airport. A process needs both plant reliability (the Process reliability tab: staying on line) and safety reliability (the protection working when it is called on), and the two can pull against each other: a second trip channel in 1oo2 cuts the dangerous failures sharply but doubles the spurious trips.

              A2 · Failure rate from a population

              λ = ΔNf / (Ns · Δt): the failures in an interval divided by the survivors at its start and the interval length. 100 identical devices (say 100 level transmitters like LT-400) are drawn from a Weibull life model R(t) = e−(t/α)β: β < 1 is burn-in, β = 1 the useful life (constant λ = 1/α, the exponential model used in the rest of this tab), β > 1 wear-out.

              A3 · R(t), PFD and proof testing

              With a constant failure rate R(t) = e−λt and PFD(t) = F(t) = 1 − e−λt ≈ λt while PFD ≪ 0.1. A trip such as LSHH-416 waits in standby, so a dangerous failure stays hidden until a demand or the next proof test, which restores it: PFDavg = (1/T)∫0Tλt dt = λT/2 (exact: 1 − (1 − e−λT)/(λT)). MTTF = ∫R dt = 1/λ.

              SIL (IEC 61511, demand mode)PFDavgRRF
              SIL 110−2 – 10−110 – 100
              SIL 210−3 – 10−2100 – 1 000
              SIL 310−4 – 10−31 000 – 10 000

              The LT-400 button shows why a generic all-modes rate is not a PFD: 1.7 /yr in λT/2 gives more than 0.5, which is why LOPA credits an alarm or a BPCS loop with a fixed typical PFD of 0.1 (B3) and a SIF with SIS-grade dangerous-undetected rates.

              A5 · The parallel-MTTF method and why LOPA differs

              Three layers against the same hazard, each with an equivalent failure rate (the sum of its blocks), combined as parallel systems through MTTF (inclusion–exclusion): 1/λsys = Σ1/λi − Σ1/(λi+λj) + 1/(λ1+λ2+λ3).

              The result is set almost entirely by the most reliable branch (the SIS). LOPA (Part B) treats the same layers differently: it multiplies the demand frequency by each layer's PFD, and it refuses credit to a layer that shares a component with the cause. On D-400 the BPCS and the alarm both hang on LT-400, so when LT-400 freezes low neither of them exists — only SIF-1 on its own sensor is left. The two methods answer different questions; show both, never pick one silently.

              A6 · Failure data used in this tab (typical values)

              EquipmentFailure mode / contextGeneric rate (/yr), typicalSIS-grade dangerous undetected (/yr), assumedUsed on D-400 for

              Generic rates count every failure mode and come from public databases of the OREDA type and the CCPS guidelines on initiating events and IPLs; SIS-grade rates count only dangerous undetected failures of certified equipment. Millions of device-hours are needed for a confident rate, so every number here is a typical value, not a vendor figure.

              Part B · Layers of protection analysis (LOPA)

              B1 · The method

              1. Take a scenario from the HAZOP (cause → consequence) and rate its severity without safeguards; the severity sets the target frequency (B2).
              2. Estimate each initiating event frequency (IEF) from failure data. When several causes lead to the same consequence, work each one and add the frequencies.
              3. Credit each independent protection layer (IPL) with its PFD. A layer that shares a component with the initiating event, or with another credited layer, gets no credit for that cause.
              4. Apply enabling conditions (the scenario needs them too) and conditional modifiers (probability of ignition, of people being present, of harm).
              5. Compare with the target: RRF = f / target. If RRF > 1 the gap sets the PFD, and so the SIL, of the extra layer.

              Worked example (textbook style). A pressure-control malfunction 0.1 /yr × high-pressure alarm with operator 0.1 × relief valve 0.01 × occupancy 0.1 = 10−5 /yr. Against a fatality target of 10−6 /yr (a stricter owner than the table below) RRF = 10: not acceptable; one more layer with PFD ≤ 0.1 (a SIL 1 trip) closes the gap.

              B2 · Criteria used here

              SeverityTarget frequency (/yr)Health and safetyEnvironmentEconomic

              Likelihood levels of the matrix below: 5 most likely (about 10 /yr), 4 likely (1), 3 possible (0.1), 2 rare (0.01), 1 almost impossible (0.001), with band limits halfway between decades. Risk = severity × likelihood: 1 negligible, 2–6 low, 8–12 medium, 15–20 high, 25 extreme. Target frequencies differ by country and owner (for a fatality about 10−4 to 10−6 /yr).

              These criteria are stricter than the HAZOP tab's ranking bands: that matrix only ranks rows for follow-up, while here every severity carries a numeric target the mitigated frequency must meet (RRF ≤ 1). The matrix picture cannot make that decision on its own: every mitigated frequency below 0.003 /yr falls in its bottom row. The worksheet therefore also places the result on the shared HAZOP/HAZID likelihood scale (1 < 10−4 … 5 > 10−1 /yr) next to the HAZOP row it came from.

              B3 · What counts as an IPL, and the time the operator has

              An IPL must be independent of the initiating event and of the other credited layers, specific to the scenario, dependable (its PFD can be justified) and auditable (tested). Procedures, training, inspection and check valves are safeguards but not IPLs. An alarm with operator response earns credit only when there is time to act — typically about 10 minutes from the alarm to the consequence.

              LayerPFD credited (typical)

              Part C · Bow-tie

              A bow-tie is several LOPAs drawn around one top event (the moment control of the hazard is lost). Threats on the left pass prevention barriers; consequences on the right sit behind mitigation (recovery) barriers and conditional modifiers. Escalation factors are conditions that defeat a barrier (a bypass, a frozen transmitter). The top-event frequency is the sum of the threat frequencies times their barrier PFDs; each consequence is compared with the target for its severity. Barrier colours follow the Safety layers tab (green BPCS, gold alarms, orange SIS, red relief, purple containment, blue emergency response); grey is a procedure (no credit) or a conditional modifier. Dashed barriers are recommended but not fitted. Click a barrier to fail it.

              1 · What a transition is, and which ones D-400 has

              Transitions are planned transient behaviour between different initial and final conditions. The plant was designed for the steady state, so a transition needs its own procedure, its own control strategy (ramps, manual outputs, permissives) and sometimes equipment that is idle the rest of the time.

              5 · Emergency trip and restart

              A trip is an unplanned transition to a safe state; the restart is a planned one from a state that is neither cold nor at design. What the SIS does (from the trip logic of the model):

              InitiatorConditionClosesReset needs

              Restart after a trip, in this order:

                6 · Maintenance transitions: take one item out, bring it back

                Equipment is taken out of service for repair, cleaning, testing or inspection. The three strategies are the same as for any regeneration: parallel or by-pass (the unit keeps running on a spare path), storage (the neighbours run from tanks while the unit is out) or shutdown.

                Task on D-400WhyHow the unit runs meanwhileHazards and how they are handledStrategy

                Return to service reverses isolation in a fixed order: work permit closed → blinds removed and recorded → N₂ purge until O₂ is below the site limit → tightness test → N₂ blanket → block valves opened with the pressure equalised → control handed back to the loop (MAN first, then AUTO when the measurement agrees with the field).

                How much storage keeps the neighbours running while D-400 is out?

                The downstream unit takes the bottoms liquid; it runs on only if a tank holds that flow for the whole outage (V = F × t). The vapour cannot be stored economically: the fuel-gas header must switch to another source. Upstream, the feed tank needs the same volume as free space, or the feed supply must also stop.

                7 · Campaign change: a new feed tank with a different composition

                When the same equipment runs several feeds, it works in blocks of steady operation separated by transitions. Product made during the transition is worth less (off-spec prices in the model: vapour , liquid USD/t instead of and ), so transitions should be short. Here the feed tank is switched at min and the new composition reaches D-400 over about 2 minutes.

                Which set points keep both specs? Steady-state runs (the Operating windows engine, all loops AUTO, trips off) over TIC-401 × PIC-420 set points. Green: AI-420 ≥ 75 and AI-410 ≤ 28 wt% at steady state (100-min runs); the outlined cell is the pair used for the campaign.

                8 · Load following: the downstream users set the rate

                A supplier that feeds consumers without storage must follow the load in time. D-400's vapour goes straight into the fuel-gas header and its liquid to the downstream unit; suppose they ask for 25 % more. The feed is moved 16 → 20 m³/h with every loop in AUTO at design set points:

                Control the result, not the sum of the demands

                The industrial rule (from steam headers): do not add up measured demands to set the supply, because every meter error accumulates and nothing corrects it; control a variable that shows the balance (a header pressure, a level, a composition) and let the supply follow it.

                PracticeSame idea on D-400

                9 · What makes transitions hard on D-400

Model limits: no thermal stress, leaks or equipment wear, no reverse flow in the product lines, ideal analysers with first-order lags.

                  Process reliability · how long D-400 runs between outages, and how to make it run longer

                  Teaching slide deck (29 slides, interactive) — reliability, availability and failure models; series, parallel, standby and k-out-of-N structures with D-400 as a series system; design, inventory, maintenance and life-cycle cost.
                  Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

                  This tab is about the reliability of production: an outage costs margin, not lives. The reliability of safeguards (probability of failure on demand, proof testing, SIL) is on the LOPA tab, and the two can pull against each other (part 5). Failure rates are typical generic all-modes values, the same as the LOPA tab's table; every fraction, repair time, off-site rate and cost marked "assumed" is a teaching value. Hold-up times, restart time, fouling limits and margins come from this page's own model.

                  1 Definitions · 2 Availability vs reliability · 3 Failure rate and the bathtub · 4 Structures · 5 D-400 as a series system · 6 Design for reliability · 7 Inventory · 8 Maintenance · 9 Life-cycle cost · 10 Flash-drum reliability audit

                  1 · Reliability, failure rate and availability: the words

                  TermDefinitionOn D-400

                  Production or safety? Reliability analysis asks "how often does the unit stop, and for how long?" and prices the answer in lost margin. Safety analysis asks "does the protection work when it is needed?" and prices the answer in risk. The same component appears in both: LSHH-416 failing safe is an outage here; failing dangerous is a PFD on the LOPA tab.

                  2 · Availability is not reliability

                  A unit that stops twelve times a year and restarts in half an hour each time has high availability and poor reliability; every stop is a trip, an off-spec restart and a disturbance passed to the fuel-gas header and the downstream unit. The same availability can come from a few long outages or many short ones.

                  3 · Failure rate, the bathtub and the Weibull model

                  The failure rate λ(t) is the number failing per unit time divided by the number still working. Over a life it often follows the bathtub: infant mortality (λ falls), chance failures (λ constant), wear-out (λ rises). Many real items show no wear-out at all, so the right maintenance depends on the pattern (part 8). With constant λ:

                  R(t) = e−λt,   F(t) = 1 − R(t),   MTTF = 1/λ

                  The Weibull model covers all three regions with one shape parameter β: R(t) = e−(t/η)β, λ(t) = (β/η)(t/η)β−1; η is the life at which 63.2 % have failed.

                  4 · Structures: series, parallel, standby, k out of N

                  A plant is many components joined in a structure, and the structure sets the system reliability. The formulas assume independent failures (no common cause) and, for standby, perfect switching.

                  StructureWorks whenReliability R(t)MTTF, N identical elements of rate λD-400 example

                  5 · D-400 as a series system: what stops the unit, and how often

                  For production every element in the chain must work: feed supply → FCV-400 → E-400 and hot oil → D-400 → level, pressure and product valves → SIS → utilities. D-400 is therefore a series system, λsys = Σ λi fi, where fi is the fraction of element i's failures that stop production (assumed). Each outage lasts the repair or switch-over time plus a restart: Tick the design options and watch the Pareto.

                  6 · Design for reliability

                  PrincipleWhat it meansD-400 as builtGap or recommendation

                  There is no safe side in equipment sizing. An oversized pump runs far left of its best-efficiency point (recirculation, vibration, seal and bearing failures); an oversized control valve works near its seat, where it is least accurate and wears fastest. At design FCV-400 is at : each valve has travel left without living at the bottom of its stroke.

                  7 · Reliability through inventory

                  Hold-up between an unreliable unit and the next lets the next unit keep running while the first is repaired. If the repair time is exponential with mean MTTR and the hold-up lasts τ = V/F, the chance that one outage is covered is 1 − e−τ/MTTR, and

                  Rsystem = R₂ [ R₁ + (1 − R₁)(1 − e−τ/MTTR) ]

                  How long D-400 itself can ride through (level hold-up from the model)

                  SituationFrom → toVolumeAtTime

                  Inventory has a price: tank cost, working capital, a larger hazardous inventory (a bigger fire case and relief load for a butane-rich liquid), and product that may age. Place hold-up next to the unreliable units and size it for their repair times, not for their trip times.

                  8 · Maintenance for reliability

                  StrategyIdeaSuits failure patternD-400 items that suit it

                  9 · Life-cycle cost: buy reliability only where it pays

                  Life-cycle costing adds to the usual profitability sum the costs that reliability changes: maintenance and spares, how often the unit fails, what each failure costs (repair, lost margin, restart) and the extra equipment bought for redundancy. Lost margin per outage hour starts at this page's own margin at design; raise it to include the downstream unit and the fuel-gas users. Capital recovery 15 %/yr and maintenance 5 %/yr of installed cost are assumed.

                  1 Efficiency and priorities · 2 D-400 now · 3 Temperature sweep · 4 Pressure sweep · 5 Both handles · 6 Feed composition · 7 E-400 fouling · 8 Heat recovery · 9 Hot-oil pumping · 10 Constraint pushing · 11 Key energy variables

                  1 · Efficiency, and where it sits among the priorities

                  Efficiency in operation means good economic performance from the equipment we have: the most valuable products from the feed, with the least energy, off-spec and loss, inside every safety and environmental limit. In operation it is the same thing as optimisation.

                  For energy, efficiency = useful energy out ÷ energy in. For a separation, the useful output is the right component in the right product: recovery = component in its product ÷ component in the feed. For the business, the measure is the margin = product value − feed − utilities.

                  Four ways to get it: design with the right capacities; use the equipment we have in its best way; choose better structures (recover heat, avoid throttling); choose the best operating conditions inside the window.

                  PriorityObjectiveOn D-400

                  Efficiency comes sixth: a margin gain never justifies a move that eats into a higher priority.

                  Chains multiply

                  The heat that ends up doing the separation passes through a chain, and the efficiencies multiply. The hot-oil heater and header are outside this simulator: their values are assumed; E-400, the drum shell and the split of the duty are the model's (live).

                  2 · D-400 now: energy, separation and economic efficiency (live)

                  Energy

                  Separation

                  Economic

                  Where the heat goes (live)

                  Enthalpies relative to the feed temperature TI-400. The hot oil through E-400 gives up the duty and goes back to its heater still hot: heat returned to the utility is not lost, it is pumped round and re-heated. What the unit buys is the duty. The oil that the 3-way valve sends round E-400 is not drawn.

                  3 · Temperature handle: TIC-401 set point from 60 to 90 °C (model)

                  Design feed 16 m³/h, 35 wt% C4, PIC-420 at 102.7 kPa g. Each point is a steady state; the product split is taken from the component balance, and the margin uses the page's prices with the off-spec prices when a specification is missed.

                  Rule of thumb (typical)What it predicts for D-400ModelWhy they differ

                  4 · Pressure handle: PIC-420 set point from 70 to 150 kPa g (model)

                  Design feed and TIC-401 at 74 °C, so the E-400 duty is the same at every point: pressure decides how that heat is shared between vapour and liquid.

                  5 · Both handles together: where the margin is best inside both specifications

                  A grid of model steady states over TIC-401 and PIC-420 set points. Each cell shows the steady margin; a cell is grey when a product is off spec. The best cell in each row sits against one specification: that is the active constraint. The principle, not a recipe: find which constraint is active, then move along it toward the better margin.

                  6 · Feed composition: the same set points give different products (model)

                  Feed butane from 25 to 45 wt% at design feed rate and pressure, at four TIC-401 set points. A lighter feed (more C4) pushes the liquid off spec; a heavier feed pushes the vapour off spec. The temperature band that keeps both products on spec moves with the feed.

                  7 · E-400 fouling: the duty stays, the hot oil pays (model)

                  Fouling lowers E-400's UA (the model's fouling fault halves it at full severity). TIC-401 holds the hot feed at 74 °C, so the duty does not change until TCV-401 runs out of travel; what changes is how much hot oil it takes and how hot the oil goes back.

                  8 · Heat recovery (design option): feed / liquid-product interchanger

                  Half of E-400's duty leaves D-400 as sensible heat in the liquid product at the flash temperature, while the feed arrives at 10 °C. A counter-current interchanger (liquid product hot side, cold feed before E-400) returns part of it. This is a design option, not part of the simulator: it is sized here by ε-NTU from the model's design streams; the model runs with a warmer feed check the E-400 side.

                  9 · Hot-oil pumping: 3-way valve by-pass or a variable-speed pump (typical estimate)

                  TCV-401 is a 3-way valve: the hot-oil pump circulates the same flow whatever E-400 takes, and the rest goes round E-400. A variable-speed drive (VSD) on a dedicated hot-oil pump would circulate only what E-400 needs. Affinity laws: flow ∝ speed, head ∝ speed², power ∝ speed³. Pump head, efficiencies and density are typical values (assumed); the flow E-400 needs comes from the model.

                  10 · Best operating conditions: push toward the active constraint

                  The best steady point sits on a specification, but the analyser value wanders about its set point. The set point must back off from the limit by enough to keep the time off spec small; less variability lets it move closer. Variability here is built from the model: analyser noise (0.05 wt%, the model's), the composition gains of part 6 times an assumed feed variability, and the temperature gain of part 3 times an assumed TIC-401 variability. Off-spec time from the normal distribution: P = ½ erfc(distance ÷ σ√2).

                  Industrial practice: reduce variability first, then move the set point; move slowly (a fast optimiser disturbs the very variables it is pushing); confirm with the model or with careful plant tests; re-check which constraint is active when prices change.

                  11 · Energy monitoring: key energy variables for D-400 (live)

                  A dashboard of the few variables that move the unit's specific energy and margin, each with its target and its effect from the model. Targets are the design values unless stated.

                  Key energy variableTargetNowEffect (model)

                  Methods: energy performance indicators and baselines as in ISO 50001 energy management; ε-NTU for the counter-current interchanger; pump affinity laws; the normal distribution for time off spec. Safety and environment come first (CCPS guidelines, OSHA 1910.119).

                  1 What an SOP is · 2 Format · 3 SOP register · 4 SOP viewer · 5 Numbers behind the steps · 6 Writing rules · 7 Life of an SOP

                  1 · What an SOP is, and which activities need one

                  A standard operating procedure is the written, approved way to carry out one task: the same steps, in the same order, with the same checks, whoever is on shift. It turns the reasons worked out on the other tabs (the start-up order, the operating window, alarm and trip limits, the hazard studies) into actions an operator can follow under pressure.

                  Process safety management (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(f)) requires written procedures for each operating phase: initial start-up; normal operations; temporary operations; emergency shutdown, including when it is required and who may order it; emergency operations; normal shutdown; start-up after a turnaround or an emergency shutdown. They must also give the operating limits, the consequences of deviation and the steps to correct or avoid it, the safety systems and their functions, and the safety and health considerations (hazards of the chemicals, exposure controls, PPE). Procedures are reviewed and certified as current every year, kept available to the people who use them, trained on, and backed by safe work practices (lock-out/tag-out, confined-space entry, opening process equipment, entry control). The Thai Department of Industrial Works regulation on process safety management carries the same elements.

                  7 · The life of an SOP

                  Draft from the design intent and the hazard studies (the HAZOP recommendations R-10, R-17, R-19, R-23 to R-28 land in these SOPs) → verify on the simulator (the graded procedures in the Exercises tab run the same steps) → review by operations, process and safety → approve and train → use, with deviations reported → review after any change (management of change), after an incident, or at the fixed interval (certified annually under 1910.119(f)(3); typically rewritten every 3 years), then re-issue.

                  References: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 (f) Operating procedures, (j) Mechanical integrity, (l) Management of change; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 Control of hazardous energy (lock-out/tag-out); CCPS, Guidelines for Writing Effective Operating and Maintenance Procedures; API 520/521 (relief and depressuring); IEC 61511 (SIS bypass and proof test); Thai Department of Industrial Works regulation on process safety management.
